Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 5–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He is the One who is capable of perfection, who is free from needing a consort and a child. Whoever is like this, it is his right to be singled out for worship, not to have partners associated with Him. By this He draws attention to the fact that He may impose on His servants whatever He wills, and He has done so.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. Al-Dahhak said: meaning, He casts this over that and that over this. This is in the linguistic sense of takwir (wrapping, i.e. casting one thing upon another), which is placing one thing on top of another. It is said: kawwara al-mata' (he piled the goods), meaning he cast some of it upon some other, and from it comes kawr al-'imamah (the winding of the turban). This meaning of the verse has also been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: what is lost from the night enters the day, and what is lost from the day enters the night. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you﴾ is a conditional clause (shart) and its response (jawab). "And He does not approve disbelief for His servants" means: if they disbelieve, that is, He does not love that from them. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: its meaning is that He does not approve disbelief for His believing servants, and they are the ones about whom Allah said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Isra: 65]. And like His saying: ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah will drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], meaning the believers. This is according to the view of those who do not distinguish between approval (al-rida') and will (al-iradah). It was also said: He does not approve disbelief even though He wills it. So Allah, exalted is He, wills disbelief from the disbeliever, and by His will he disbelieved, yet He does not approve it nor love it. Thus He wills the existence of what He does not approve, and Allah, mighty and majestic, willed the creation of Iblis while He does not approve of him. So will is other than approval. This is the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ means: He approves gratitude for you, because "you are grateful" (tashkuru) indicates it. The discussion of gratitude has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 397 and following, second or third printing, and vol. 2, p. 172, second printing] and elsewhere. "Yarda" here means "yuthibu wa yuthni" (rewards and praises). So the approval, in this sense, is either His reward, and then it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l), as in ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]; or His praise, and then it is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat). The reading of "yarduhu" with sukun on the ha' was recited by Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr, Shaybah and Hubayrah from 'Asim. Ibn Dhakwan, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Kisa'i and Warsh from Nafi' gave the damma full vowel (ishba'), and the rest used the short vowel (ikhtilas).

﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts﴾ has been discussed in more than one place [see vol. 7, p. 157, first or second printing, and vol. 10, p. 230, first or second printing].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 8–9:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When harm touches man﴾, meaning the disbeliever, "harm" means hardship from poverty and affliction. ﴿He calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾, meaning returning to Him, humbling himself, obeying Him, and seeking His help to remove that hardship from him. ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favour from Himself﴾, meaning He gives him and grants him possession. It is said: "Allah granted you (khawwalaka) the thing," meaning He made you its owner. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used to recite:

"There, if they are given wealth in loan, they lend (yukhawwilu)... and if they ask, they are given, and if they gamble, they win (yughlu)."

[[The verse is attributed to Zuhayr. It is also narrated as: "There, if they seek loans of wealth, they lend." Al-ikhyal means lending, that is, they lend a she-camel for its milk and wool, and a horse for raiding upon it. "If they gamble (yayassiru), they win (yughlu)" means that when they cast lots in the game of maysir, they take the fattened camels they wagered upon.]]

And the khawal of a man is his household servants; the singular is khail. Abu al-Najm said:

"He gives and does not withhold, and withholds... and heaps up the summits from the servants of the one who has been granted."

﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾, meaning he forgets the Lord whom he used to call upon before, so that the harm is removed from him. According to this interpretation, "ma" refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, and is in the sense of "alladhi" (who). It is also said that "ma" is in the sense of "man" (who), as in His saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 3], and the meaning is the same. It is also said: he forgot the supplication with which he used to humble himself before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning he abandoned the fact that the supplication was directed to Allah. On this view, "ma" and the verb form a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿And he sets up rivals to Allah﴾, meaning idols and images. Al-Suddi said: it means rivals from among men, whom they rely upon in all their affairs. ﴿To lead astray from His way﴾, meaning so that the ignorant may follow him. ﴿Say: enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾, meaning say to this person, "Enjoy," and this is an imperative of threat, for the enjoyments of this world are few. ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning your final destination is the Fire.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾. Exalted is He has shown that the believer is not like the disbeliever mentioned earlier. Al-Hasan, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read "Amman" with a shadda (doubled m). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and Hamzah read "Amman huwa" without the shadda, in the sense of a vocative, as if he said: "O one who is devoutly obedient." Al-Farra' said: the alif is in the position of "ya" (O). You say: "Ya Zayd, aqbil" and "Azayd, aqbil." This is reported from Sibawayh and all the grammarians, as Aws ibn Hajar said:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand, and no hand that lacks a forearm..."

Another poet, Dhu al-Rummah, said:

"Did the abode at Huzwa stir in the eye a tear, and did the water of love flow or trickle?"

According to this reading, the sense is: "Say: enjoy your disbelief for a little while, indeed you are of the companions of the Fire, O one who is devoutly obedient, indeed you are of the companions of Paradise." This is like someone saying: "So-and-so does not pray and does not fast," and then: "O you who pray and fast, rejoice!" The second clause is omitted because the context indicates it. It is also said that the alif in "Amman" is an interrogative alif, meaning: "Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night (better)? Or one who sets up rivals to Allah?" The implied meaning is: the one who is devoutly obedient is better. As for the one who doubled the m in "Amman," the meaning is: the disobedient ones mentioned before are better than "Amman huwa qanit," and the clause that is the counterpart of "am" is omitted, the original being "am man," which was assimilated into the m. Al-Nahhas said: "am" means "bal" (rather), and "man" means "alladhi" (who), and the sense is: "Or is the one who is devoutly obedient better than the one mentioned?"

The word qanit (devoutly obedient) has four possible meanings. The first is that it means one who obeys, as said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second is that it means one who is humble in his prayer, as said by Ibn Shihab. The third is that it means one who stands in his prayer, as said by Yahya ibn Sallam. The fourth is that it means one who supplicates to his Lord. Ibn Mas'ud's view includes all of these. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Every qunut (devout obedience) in the Qur'an is obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic." It was also narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he was asked which prayer is best, and he said: "Long qunut." A group of scholars interpreted this as long standing. 'Abd Allah narrated from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he was asked about qunut and said: "I know qunut only as long standing and reciting the Qur'an." Mujahid said: among the forms of qunut are a long bowing and lowering the gaze. When the scholars stood in prayer, they lowered their gaze, humbled themselves, did not turn their heads in their prayer, did not play, and did not mention any matter of this world except forgetfully. Al-Nahhas said: the origin of this is that qunut means obedience, so everything that is said about it is obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. All these things fall within obedience, and so do other things, as Nafi' said: Ibn 'Umar said to me, "Stand and pray." So I stood to pray, and I had a worn garment. He called me and said to me: "What do you think, if I sent you on some errand, would you go like this?" I said: "I would adorn myself." He said: "Then Allah is more deserving that you adorn yourself for Him."

There is disagreement about the identity of the qanit here. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned that it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of al-Dahhak from him, said: it is Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ibn 'Umar said: it is 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. Muqatil said: it is 'Ammar ibn Yasir. Al-Kalbi said: it is Suhayb, Abu Dharr and Ibn Mas'ud. Also from al-Kalbi, it is related in a mursal form, concerning whoever is in this state.

﴿During the hours of the night﴾. Al-Hasan said: its periods, its beginning, its middle and its end. From Ibn 'Abbas: "during the hours of the night" means the middle of the night. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever wishes that Allah make the standing on the Day of Resurrection easy for him, let him be seen by Allah in the darkness of the night prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord. It is also said: it means between Maghrib and 'Isha'. Al-Hasan's view is general.

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿And hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, that is, the blessings of Paradise. It was narrated from al-Hasan that he was asked about a man who persists in sins and hopes, and he said: "This one is merely wishful."

Whoever reads "Amman" with the lightened alif (as a vocative) does not pause at "the mercy of his Lord," because His saying, "Say: are those who know equal to those who do not know?" is connected to it, unless one assumes an ellipsis in the speech, which is easier, as explained earlier. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, so too the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. Others said: "those who know" are those who benefit from their knowledge and act upon it, whereas whoever does not benefit from his knowledge and does not act upon it is in the position of one who has no knowledge.

﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾, that is, the people of intellect among the believers.

﴿Fearing the Hereafter﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿And hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, that is, the blessings of Paradise. It was narrated from al-Hasan that he was asked about a man who persists in sins and hopes, and he said: "This one is merely wishful."

Whoever reads "Amman" with the lightened alif (as a vocative) does not pause at "the mercy of his Lord," because His saying, "Say: are those who know equal to those who do not know?" is connected to it, unless one assumes an ellipsis in the speech, which is easier, as explained earlier. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, so too the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. Others said: "those who know" are those who benefit from their knowledge and act upon it, whereas whoever does not benefit from his knowledge and does not act upon it is in the position of one who has no knowledge.

﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾, that is, the people of intellect among the believers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 10:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O My servants who have believed﴾, meaning: say, O Muhammad, to My believing servants: ﴿fear your Lord﴾, meaning: fear His disobediences. The tā' (in ittaqū) is substituted from a wāw, and this has already been discussed [[See vol. 1, p. 161, second or third edition.]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and those who emigrated with him to Abyssinia. Then He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. By the first "good" (ḥasanah) is meant obedience, and by the second, the reward in Paradise. It has also been said: the meaning is, for those who do good in this world there is good in this world, which is in addition to the reward of the Hereafter. The additional good in this world is health, well-being, victory, and spoils. Al-Qushayri said: the first view is more correct, because the disbelievers too have attained the blessings of this world. I say: the believer also attains them along with it, and his Paradise is increased when he gives thanks for those blessings. Good in this world may also be good repute, and in the Hereafter, recompense. ﴿And Allah's earth is spacious﴾, so emigrate within it, and do not remain with those who practise disobedience. This matter has already been fully discussed in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, pp. 348 onward, first or second edition.]]. It has also been said: what is meant is the land of Paradise; He encourages them with its vastness and the vastness of its bliss, as He said: ﴿whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. Paradise is also called an earth, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and given us the earth to inherit, that we may settle in Paradise wherever we will."﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. But the first view is more apparent, for it is a command to emigrate, i.e., depart from Makkah to wherever you may be safe. Al-Mawardi said: it is possible that by the vastness of the earth is meant the vastness of provision, because He provides for them from the earth, so the meaning would be: "and Allah's provision is vast." This is closer to the sense, because He expressed its vastness as a favour. I say: the verse is then evidence for moving from an expensive land to a cheaper land, as Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Be in a place where you can fill your sack with bread for a dirham." ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾, i.e., without reckoning. It has also been said: it is increased upon the reward, because if they were given according to the measure of what they did, it would be by reckoning. It has also been said: "without measure" means without follow-up and without demand, as the demand occurs for the pleasures of this world. Here "the patient" (al-ṣābirūn) means the fasting ones; the evidence for this is the statement of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), reporting from Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "Fasting is for Me and I shall reward it." The scholars said: every reward is measured by volume and weighed by weight, except fasting, which is given by handfuls and scooped by scoops. This is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Malik ibn Anas said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾: it is patience upon the calamities and griefs of this world. There is no doubt that everyone who submits to what befalls him and abandons what he has been forbidden, their reward has no measure. Qatadah said: "No, by Allah, there is no measure or balance there." Anas narrated to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The scales will be set up, and the people of charity will be brought and their rewards given to them by the scales; and likewise prayer and pilgrimage. The people of trials will be brought, and no scale will be set up for them, nor will a register be spread out for them, and the reward will be poured upon them without reckoning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾, until the people of well-being in this world wish that their bodies were being cut with scissors, because of the excellence the people of trials receive." And from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard my grandfather, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), say: "Perform the obligations and you will be among the most devout of people; and hold to contentment and you will be among the richest of people. O my son, indeed in Paradise there is a tree called the Tree of Trial. The people of trials will be brought, and no scale will be set up for them, nor will a register be spread out for them; the reward will be poured upon them in abundance." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾. The word ṣābir is praised, but it applies only to one who is patient in refraining from disobedience; if you wish to say that he is patient in face of a calamity, you say ṣābir 'alā kadhā (patient upon such-and-such). Al-Nahhas said. This has already passed in "al-Baqarah."

Completed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 11–16:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion."﴾ It has been mentioned at the beginning of the surah: "And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims" from this ummah. Likewise, he was. He was the first to oppose the religion of his fathers, to renounce the idols and smash them, to submit to Allah and believe in Him, and to call to Him ﷺ. The lam in His words "li-an akuna" (in "that I should be") is a superfluous connective particle, as said by al-Jurjani and others. It was also said that it is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajl). There is an omission in the statement, meaning: I have been commanded to worship "that I should be the first of the Muslims." He means the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. He said this when his people invited him to the religion of his fathers. Abu Hamza al-Thumali and Ibn al-Musayyab said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. So this verse was revealed before the sins of the Prophet ﷺ were forgiven.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion."﴾ "Allah" is in the accusative case, governed by "a'bud" (I worship). "Sincere to Him in my religion" means my obedience and my worship. ﴿So worship what you will besides Him.﴾ This is an imperative of threat, warning and reproach, like His words: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. It was also said that it is a command of the sword verse.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ Maymun ibn Mihran reported from Ibn Abbas: There is no one for whom Allah has not created a wife in Paradise; so when he enters the Fire, he has lost himself and his family. In another report from Ibn Abbas: whoever acts in obedience to Allah, he will have that dwelling and that family, except what had been his before that, and this is His words: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10].

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿For them there will be layers of Fire above them and layers below them.﴾ He called what is beneath them "zulal" (layers) because it shades those beneath them. This verse is similar to His words: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and over them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41], and His words: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. ﴿That is what Allah makes fear His servants.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: His allies (awliya'). ﴿O My servants, so fear Me.﴾ That is, O My allies, so fear Me. It was also said: it is general, applying to both the believer and the disbeliever. And it was said: it is specific to the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 17–18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who avoid the Taghut (idols/false deities), not worshipping them﴾. Al-Akhfash said: "Al-Taghut is a plural noun, and it is permissible for it to be a singular feminine noun." It has already been discussed [[See vol. 5, p. 280, first or second edition.]]. That is, they kept away from the Taghut and were on its side, so they did not worship it. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: it is the Shaytan (Satan). Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is the idols. It was also said: it is the soothsayer (kahin). It was also said that it is a non-Arabic name, like Talut, Jalut, Harut and Marut. It was also said: it is an Arabic name derived from tughyan (transgression). The particle "an" (that) is in a position of accusative as a substitute (badal) for "al-Taghut," its meaning being: "And those who avoided the worship of the Taghut."

﴿And turned in repentance to Allah﴾, that is, they returned to His worship and obedience. ﴿For them is good news﴾ in the life of this world, of Paradise in the hereafter. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Uthman, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd, Sa'id, Talhah and al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, who asked Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and he informed them of his faith, so they believed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and Abu Dharr and others who affirmed the oneness of Allah the Exalted before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿So give good news to My servants, those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it is the man who hears the good and the bad, so he speaks of the good and refrains from the bad, so he does not speak of it. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an and other things, and they follow the Qur'an. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an and the sayings of the Messenger, and they follow its best, that is, its muhkam (clear, definitive), so they act upon it. It was also said: they listen to resolve (azm) and concession (tarkhis), and they take the resolve rather than the concession. It was also said: they listen to the obligatory punishment due to them and to pardon, and they take the pardon. It was also said: the best word, for one who holds that the verse refers to those who affirmed the oneness of Allah before Islam, is "There is no god but Allah."

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and Salman al-Farisi. They avoided the Taghut from worshipping it in their pre-Islamic ignorance, and they followed the best of what came to them of speech.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ to what He is pleased with. ﴿And those are the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, that is, the people of intellect among the believers who benefited from their minds.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and Abu Dharr and others who affirmed the oneness of Allah the Exalted before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿So give good news to My servants, those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it is the man who hears the good and the bad, so he speaks of the good and refrains from the bad, so he does not speak of it. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an and other things, and they follow the Qur'an. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an and the sayings of the Messenger, and they follow its best, that is, its muhkam (clear, definitive), so they act upon it. It was also said: they listen to resolve (azm) and concession (tarkhis), and they take the resolve rather than the concession. It was also said: they listen to the obligatory punishment due to them and to pardon, and they take the pardon. It was also said: the best word, for one who holds that the verse refers to those who affirmed the oneness of Allah before Islam, is "There is no god but Allah."

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and Salman al-Farisi. They avoided the Taghut from worshipping it in their pre-Islamic ignorance, and they followed the best of what came to them of speech.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ to what He is pleased with. ﴿And those are the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, that is, the people of intellect among the believers who benefited from their minds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 19:

Allah's words: ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due—will you, then, save those who are in the Fire?﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) used to be eager for the faith of a people for whom Allah had already decreed wretchedness, so this verse was revealed.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to Abu Lahab, his son, and those of the Prophet's (ﷺ) kin who stayed away from faith.

He repeated the interrogative in His words "afa-anta" (will you, then) for emphasis, due to the length of the speech. Sibawayh likewise said this about Allah's words: ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35], according to what has preceded [see vol. 12, p. 122, first or second edition].

The meaning is: "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due" — will you, then, save him? The sentence has a conditional (shart) and its response (jawab). The interrogative was used to indicate reproach (tawqif) and affirmation (taqrir).

al-Farra' said: The meaning is "Will you, then, save those against whom the word of punishment has become due?" and the meaning is the same.

It is also said that there is an ellipsis (hadhf) in the sentence, and the estimated sense is: "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due—will he escape from it?" and what follows is a new clause (mustaʼnaf). He said "afa-man haqqa 'alayhi" and in another place said: ﴿The word of punishment has become due﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], because when the verb comes first and there is a separation between it and its feminine subject, both masculine and feminine forms are permitted. However, the feminine here is not real; rather, "kalimah" means "kalam" and "qawl," i.e., "Is then one upon whom the saying of punishment has become due."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾. When He explained that the disbelievers have layers of fire above them and layers below them, He explained that for the God-fearing (muttaqin) there are lofty chambers (ghuraf), above which are further chambers, because Paradise has ranks (darajat), some of which rise above others. And "lakin" (but) here is not for istidrak (correction of a preceding negation), because there was no negation before it, as in your saying: "I did not see Zayd, but ʿAmr." Rather, it is for moving from one account (qissa) to another account that differs from the first, as in your saying: "Zayd came to me, but ʿAmr did not come."

"Ghuraf mabniyyah" (built chambers). Ibn ʿAbbas said: of emerald (zabarjad) and ruby (yaqut). "Beneath which rivers flow": that is, they comprise the means of delight.

"Promise of Allah" (wa'd Allah) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "for them are chambers" is that Allah promised them that as a promise. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, with the meaning: that is the promise of Allah.

"Allah does not break the promise" (la yukhlifu Allah al-mi'ad): that is, He does not fail what He promised to both groups.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾. That is, He does not fail in His promise regarding the reviving of creation and the distinguishing between the believer and the disbeliever, and He is able to do that just as He is able to send down water from the sky. "Sends down from the sky" means from the clouds, "water" means rain. "Then He makes it flow" means He makes it enter into the earth and dwell in it, as He said: ﴿Then We caused it to settle in the earth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18]. "Springs" (yanabi') is the plural of yanbu' (spring), which is on the pattern of yafu'ul, from nabaa, yanbu', yanba' and yanbi', in the nominative, accusative and genitive cases. Al-Nahhas said: Ibn Kaysan related to us regarding the saying of the poet [[The poet is 'Antarah. It is also narrated as "ghadub hurrah." Its completion is: "zayyafatun mithl al-fanīq al-muqram"]]:

yanba'u min dhifra ghadubin jasratin

that its meaning is yanbu', and he lengthened the fatha so it became an alif, nubuwan (it gushed forth). The yanbu' is the eye (source) of water, and its plural is al-yanabi'. This has already been discussed under "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 330, first or second edition.]]. "Then He brings forth by it" means by that water emerging from the springs of the earth, "crops" (zar') which is a collective noun, meaning various crops of different colours: red, yellow, blue, green, and so on. Al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak said: Every water in the earth has come down from the sky; it descends from the sky onto the rock, and then the springs and wells are divided from it. "Then it dries up" means it becomes dry. "Then you see it" means after its greenness "yellowed." Al-Mubarrad said: al-Asma'i said: It is said that the land "hāja" (dries up) when its vegetation has turned away and departed. He said: Thus the plant "hāja." He said: Thus said others besides al-Asma'i. Al-Jawhari said: The plant "hāja" hiyājan, meaning it dried out. A "hā'ija" land is one whose herbage has dried or yellowed; the wind "ahāja" the plant, meaning it dried it out; "ahyajna al-ard" means we found the land with plants that had dried; "hāja hā'ijuhu" means his anger was stirred; "hada'a hā'ijuhu" means his agitation calmed. "Then He makes it debris" means broken fragments, from "taḥaṭṭama al-'ūd" when the wood crumbles from dryness. The meaning is that whoever is able to do this is able to restore. It has also been said: this is a parable Allah struck for the Qur'an and for the breasts of those on the earth, meaning: He sent down from the sky a Qur'an and caused it to flow into the hearts of the believers. "Then He brings forth by it crops of varying colours" means a religion of varying degrees, some of it more excellent than others; as for the believer, his faith and certainty increase, and as for the one in whose heart is a disease, he withers as the crop withers. It has also been said: this is a parable Allah struck for the worldly life, meaning just as the green plant changes and turns yellow, so is the world after its brightness. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 22:

Sharaha means he opened and widened. Ibn 'Abbas said: He widened his breast for Islam until it became firm in it. As-Suddi said: "with Islam," for joy in it and tranquillity in it. According to this view, this expansion can only occur after Islam. According to the first view, the expansion may occur before Islam.

﴿So is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord...﴾ means: upon guidance from his Lord, as opposed to one whose heart Allah has sealed and hardened. The omitted part is indicated by His words: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened...﴾ Al-Mubarrad said: One says qasa al-qalb (the heart hardened) when it became stiff. Likewise 'ataa and 'asa are close to it. A qalb qasin is a stiff heart that does not soften or yield.

The one whom Allah has expanded the breast of, here, according to what the exegetes mention, is 'Ali and Hamza, may Allah be pleased with them both. An-Naqqash related that it was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Muqatil said: 'Ammar ibn Yasir. Also from him and from al-Kalbi: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The verse is general for whoever Allah expands the breast of by creating faith in it.

Murrah [[This is Murrah ibn Sharahil al-Hamdani, who narrated from Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, Abu Dharr, Hudhayfah, Ibn Mas'ud, etc. ... al-Tahdhib.]] narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, regarding His saying, ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord...﴾, how is the breast expanded?" He said: "When the light enters the heart, it expands and opens." We said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning toward the Abode of Eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before its descent."

At-Tirmidhi al-Hakim recorded it in Nawadir al-Usul from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: A man said, "O Messenger of Allah, which of the believers is most discerning?" He said: "The one who remembers death most, and is best prepared for it. When the light enters the heart, it becomes open and wide." They said: "What is the sign of that, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "Turning toward the Abode of Eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death descends." So he (ﷺ) mentioned three qualities. There is no doubt that whoever has these qualities is one of perfect faith. Turning toward the Abode is only righteous deeds, because the Abode of Eternity was only prepared as a reward for righteous deeds. Do you not see how Allah mentioned it in various places in His revelation, then said right after that: ﴿a reward for what they used to do﴾? So Paradise is the reward for deeds. When the servant constricts himself in righteous deeds, that is his turning toward the Abode of Eternity. When his greed for the world subsides and his concern for it fades, and he turns to what suffices him from it, so he is content and satisfied, then he has withdrawn from the abode of delusion. When he firmly arranges his affairs with piety, so that he looks into every matter, standing, courteous, cautious, wary, withdrawing from what casts doubt on him to what does not cast doubt on him, then he has prepared for death. These are their signs outwardly. This state arises only from the light that has entered the heart.

As for His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾: it was said that the intended referent is Abu Lahab and his sons. The meaning of "min dhikr Allah" (against the remembrance of Allah) is that their hearts increase in hardness from hearing His remembrance. It was also said that "man" here means "'an" (from), so the meaning is that they hardened against accepting the remembrance of Allah. This is the choice of at-Tabari.

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Jadri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted said: Seek your needs from the generous, for I have placed My mercy in them, and do not seek them from those whose hearts are hard, for I have placed My wrath in them."

Malik ibn Dinar said: No servant has been struck with a punishment greater than the hardness of heart. Allah has not been angry with a people such that He removed mercy from their hearts.

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, "Allah has sent down the best discourse" (nazzala ahsan al-hadith), meaning the Qur'an. When He said, "who listen to the word and follow the best of it" (fa-yattabi'una ahsanahu), He made clear that the best of what is heard is what Allah has sent down, namely the Qur'an. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "If only you would relate to us," and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down, "Allah has sent down the best discourse." Then they said, "If only you would narrate to us," and it was sent down, "We relate to you the best of narratives." Then they said, "If only you would admonish us," and it was sent down, "Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should become humble to the remembrance of Allah?" to the end of the verse.

It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grew weary, so they said to him, "Relate to us," and it was revealed.

Al-hadith is what the narrator relates. The Qur'an is called hadith because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to relate it to his Companions and his people. This is like His saying, "Then in what statement after this will they believe?" and His saying, "Do you wonder at this statement?" and His saying, "So leave Me with the one who denies this statement" [al-Qalam: 44].

Al-Qushayri said: Some people imagined that hadith derives from hudūth (being created, originated), and so it would indicate that His speech is created. This is an illusion, because the word hadith is not used in that sense in His saying, "No reminder comes to them from their Lord that is newly revealed (muhdath)." It has been said that hudūth refers to the recitation, not to what is recited, just as the remembrance refers to the one remembered when we mention the names of the Lord, exalted is He.

"Kitaban" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ahsan al-hadith," and it may also be a circumstantial (hal) of it.

"Mutashabihan" means that some of it resembles other parts in excellence and wisdom, and confirms other parts; there is no contradiction or discord in it. Qatadah said: it resembles itself in its verses and letters. It has also been said: it resembles the books of Allah sent down to His prophets, in that it contains command, prohibition, encouragement and warning, although it is more general and more inimitable.

Then He described it: "mathani" (oft-repeated), meaning that stories, admonitions and rulings are repeated in it; and it is repeated for recitation so that it is not wearisome.

"Taqsha'irru" means they tremble and are stirred by fear of what it contains of threat. "Then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah": that is, at the verse of mercy. It has also been said: towards acting upon the Book of Allah and affirming it. It has been said too: "to the remembrance of Allah" means Islam.

The second issue: It is related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that she said: When the Qur'an was recited to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), as Allah had described them, their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver. It was said to her: "Indeed, some people today, when the Qur'an is recited to them, one of them falls down unconscious." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan."

Sa'id ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Jumahi said: Ibn Umar passed by a man from among the people of the Qur'an who had collapsed, and he said, "What is wrong with this one?" They said, "When the Qur'an is recited to him and he hears the remembrance of Allah, he falls." Ibn Umar said, "We fear Allah, and we do not fall." Then he said, "Indeed, Shaytan enters into the inside of one of them. This was not the practice of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: The people who fall into a seizure when the Qur'an is recited to them were mentioned in the presence of Ibn Sirin, and he said, "Between us and them is this: let one of them sit on the roof of a house with his legs outstretched, then let the Qur'an be recited to him from beginning to end. If he throws himself down, then he is truthful."

Abu Imran al-Jawni said: Musa (peace be upon him) once admonished the Children of Israel, and a man tore his shirt. Allah revealed to Musa, "Tell the owner of the shirt not to tear his shirt, for I do not love the wasteful; he is splitting open his heart to Me."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b wept in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him were his Companions, and they wept too. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Seize the opportunity of supplication at the time of tenderness, for it is mercy."

It is related from al-Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the skin of a believer shivers out of fear of Allah, his sins fall away from him as the withered leaves fall from a dry tree."

It is related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant's skin shivers out of fear of Allah except that Allah forbids it to the Fire."

It is related from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm al-Darda', who said: "Fear in the heart of a man is only like the burning of a palm frond. Do you not find only a shivering?" I said, "Yes." She said, "Then call upon Allah, for supplication at that moment is answered."

It is related from Thabit al-Bunani that he said: A certain man said, "I know when my supplication will be answered." They said, "How do you know that?" He said, "When my skin shivers, my heart trembles, and my eyes overflow, that is the moment when my supplication is answered."

It is said: "iqsha'arra jild al-rajul" (the man's skin shivered), with the verbal noun "iqsh‘irar"; he is "muqsha'irr," and the plural is "qasha'ir," in which the mim is dropped because it is an augment. One says: "akhadhathu qusha'iriyya" (a shivering seized him). Imru' al-Qays said:

"So I spent the night struggling with the longest night of winter, and the heart, from fear, was shivering."

It has been said: since the Qur'an was at the utmost in eloquence and rhetoric, whenever they saw their inability to produce its like, their skins shivered before it, out of exalting it and wonder at the excellence of its composition, and awe at what it contains. This is like His saying, exalted is He: "Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from the fear of Allah" [al-Hashr: 21]. So splitting apart is close to shivering, and humility is close to His saying, "then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah." The meaning of the softening of the heart is its tenderness, its tranquillity and its calm.

"That is the guidance of Allah" (dhalika huda Allah): that is, the Qur'an is the guidance of Allah. It has also been said: that which Allah granted to these people, from fear of His punishment and hope in His reward, is the guidance of Allah.

"And whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him" (wa-man yudlil Allah fa-ma lahu min hadin): that is, whomever He forsakes, there is no one to guide him. This refutes the Qadariyya and others.

The meaning of all of this has already been fully explained in more than one place, and praise be to Allah.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin paused on His saying "hadin" in both places with a yā' (hādī), while the rest read it without the yā'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 24–26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment⦆ (39:24). ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Zayd said: He will be thrown into the Fire bound, and the first thing the Fire touches of him will be his face. Mujahid said: He will be dragged on his face in the Fire. Muqatil said: It is that the disbeliever is thrown into the Fire with his hands chained to his neck, and on his neck is a great rock like a huge mountain of sulfur. The Fire kindles in the rock while it hangs on his neck, so its heat and its blaze fall upon his face, and he cannot push it away from his face because of the shackles. The predicate is omitted. Al-Akhfash said: That is, ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment⦆ better, or one who is made happy, like: ﴿Is one who is cast into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?⦆ (41:40). And it was said: ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers⦆, that is, the guardians will say to the disbelievers: ﴿Taste what you used to earn⦆, that is, the recompense of your earning of sins. A similar verse is: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard⦆ (9:35).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive. So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world⦆. Its meaning has already been mentioned (see vol. 2, p. 79, second edition). Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever reaches a bodily organ of something is said to have "tasted" it, that is, it arrives at it just as sweetness and bitterness reach the one who tastes them. He said: Khizy (disgrace) is from what is disliked, and khaza'a (shame) is from feeling shy. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater⦆, that is, than what befell them in this world, ﴿if only they knew⦆.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 27–28:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾, that is, every kind of example they need, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said: what We have mentioned of the destruction of the earlier nations is an example for these people. "So that they may be mindful" means that they may take warning. "An Arabic Qur'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Al-Akhfash said: because His saying, Majestic and Mighty, "in this Qur'an" is definite. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "Arabic" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, and "Qur'an" is a preparatory introduction to the circumstantial qualifier, just as you say, "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man," so your saying "righteous" (ṣāliḥan) is the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. Al-Zajjaj said: "Arabic" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, and "Qur'an" is an emphatic appositive. "Without any crookedness" (ghayra dhī ʿiwaj). Al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about it is the saying of al-Dahhak, who said: "not divergent." This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. And from Ibn ʿAbbas also: "not created," mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Suddi said it as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "not contradictory." Mujahid said: "without ambiguity." He said:

And there has come to you a certainty without crookedness... and a word from God that is not false.

"So that they may be God-fearing" (laʿallahum yattaqun): from disbelief and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 27–28:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾, that is, every kind of example they need, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said: what We have mentioned of the destruction of the earlier nations is an example for these people. "So that they may be mindful" means that they may take warning. "An Arabic Qur'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Al-Akhfash said: because His saying, Majestic and Mighty, "in this Qur'an" is definite. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "Arabic" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, and "Qur'an" is a preparatory introduction to the circumstantial qualifier, just as you say, "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man," so your saying "righteous" (ṣāliḥan) is the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. Al-Zajjaj said: "Arabic" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, and "Qur'an" is an emphatic appositive. "Without any crookedness" (ghayra dhī ʿiwaj). Al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about it is the saying of al-Dahhak, who said: "not divergent." This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. And from Ibn ʿAbbas also: "not created," mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Suddi said it as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "not contradictory." Mujahid said: "without ambiguity." He said:

And there has come to you a certainty without crookedness... and a word from God that is not false.

"So that they may be God-fearing" (laʿallahum yattaqun): from disbelief and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 29:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners quarreling with one another﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: "rajulan" is in the accusative because it is an explanation (tarjamah) of "mathalan" and an elaboration of it. If you wish, you may put it in the accusative by removing the preposition; its meaning would be: Allah presents an example with a man "in whom are partners quarreling with one another." Al-Farra' said: that is, "mukhtalifun" (disagreeing). Al-Mubarrad said: that is, "mut'asiruna" (difficult to deal with), from shakisa yashkusu shukson, on the pattern of qufl, so he is shakis, like 'asura ya'suru 'usran, so he is 'asir. It is said: a man who is shakis, sharis, dharis and dabis. It is also said: a man who is dabs and dabis, meaning sharis, 'asir, shakis, as stated by al-Jawhari. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-tashakus and al-tasharkhus mean disagreement. It is said: his affairs became tashakasat, and his teeth tasharkhasat. It is also said: Fulan shakasani, meaning he haggled with me and contended with me over my right. Al-Jawhari said: a man who is shakṣ with a sukun, meaning difficult in character. The rajiz said:

shaksun 'abusun 'anbasun 'adhawwar

And a people who are shuks, on the pattern of rajul sidq and qawm sidq. Shakisa with a kasra means shakasah. Al-Farra' related: rajul shaks, and this is the analogical form. This is the example of one who worships many deities. "Wa rajulan salaman li-rajul," meaning sincerely devoted to one master, and this is the example of one who worships Allah alone. "Hal yastawiyan mathalan" (Are the two equal in likeness?). This is one who serves a group of partners whose characters differ and whose intentions vary; every man who meets him pulls him and makes him serve, so he suffers hardship, fatigue and great exhaustion from them, and despite all this he pleases none of them with his service because of the multitude of rights upon him. But the one who serves one master, whom no one contests with him, when he obeys him alone, he recognises that for him, and if he errs, he overlooks his error. So which of the two is less burdened, or upon the straight guidance?

The people of Kufa and the people of Medina read: "wa rajulan salaman." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Asim al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read: "wa rajulan salimان" (wa rajulan salimًا). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading for the soundness of its interpretation. He said: because "salim" means pure, the opposite of shared, while "salam" is the opposite of war, and there is no place for war here. Al-Nahhas said: this argument is not binding, because when a word has two meanings it is to be understood only in its more appropriate sense. Although "salam" is the opposite of war, it has another place, as one says to you, "in this dwelling there are partners," so it became "salam" for you. And the same objection applies to "salim" as applied to the others, because one says "shay'un salim," meaning it has no defect. Both readings are good, and the leading authorities recited both. Abu Hatim preferred the reading of the people of Medina, "salaman," and said: this is beyond dispute. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah and Nasr read "silman," with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. "Salaman" and "silman" are both verbal nouns (masadir), and the implied phrase is: "wa rajulan dha silmin," the qualifier being omitted. "Mathalan" is a specification of manner (tamyiz); the meaning is: are their attributes and conditions equal? Only a single specification was given for the sake of clarifying the category.

"Al-hamdu lillah, bal aktharuhum la ya'lamun" (Praise be to Allah; but most of them do not know), that is, the truth, so that they may follow it.

Ibn Muhayṣin, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "innaka māʾitun wa-innahum māʾitūn" (إِنَّكَ مَائِتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَائِتُونَ), and it is a good reading; ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr also recited it thus. Al-Nahhas said: Such an alif is dropped in the irregular readings, and "māʾit" in the future sense is frequent in the speech of the Arabs. Similar to it is "kāna marīḍan" and "innahu la-māriḍun min hadha al-taʿām" (he is indeed ill from this food).

Al-Hasan, al-Farraʾ and al-Kisaʾi said: al-mayyit with a shadda (mayyit) is one who has not yet died but will die, and al-mayt with a light pronunciation (mayt) is one from whom the soul has departed. For this reason it is not lightened here.

Qatadah said: His own death was announced to the Prophet ﷺ, and your deaths were announced to you.

Thabit al-Bunani said: A man informed Silah ibn Ashyam of the death of a brother of his, and he found him eating. He said: "Come and eat, for my brother was announced to me some time ago." He said: "How (can that be), when I am the first to bring you the news?" He said: "Allah the Exalted announced him to me, saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾."

This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, informing him of his death and their death, and it admits of five aspects:

First, that this is a warning concerning the Hereafter.

Second, that it is mentioned as an incitement to action.

Third, that it is mentioned as a preparation for death.

Fourth, so that they do not dispute about his death as the nations disputed about other prophets. Indeed, when ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, denied his death, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with this verse, and he fell silent.

Fifth, to let him know that Allah the Exalted has made all His creatures equal in it, despite their differences in other matters, so that consolation may be abundant in it and grief may be little in it.

﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute﴾, meaning the disputing of the disbeliever and the believer, and the oppressor and the oppressed; so said Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

And in a lengthy report: Indeed, the dispute will reach, on the Day of Resurrection, to the point that the soul disputes with the body.

Al-Zubayr said: When this verse was revealed, we said: "O Messenger of Allah, will what was between us in this world be repeated upon us, along with the particular sins?" He said: "Yes, it will indeed be repeated upon you until every possessor of a right is given his right." Al-Zubayr then said: "By Allah, the matter is indeed severe."

Ibn ʿUmar said: We lived a span of our lives thinking that this verse was revealed concerning us and the People of the Two Books: ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute﴾. We said: "How shall we dispute, when our Prophet is one, and our religion is one?" until I saw some of us striking the faces of others with the sword, and I knew that it was revealed concerning us.

Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said: We used to say, "Our Lord is one, our religion is one, and our Prophet is one; so what is this dispute?" Then when the day of Siffin came and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: "Yes, this is it."

Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: When this verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began to say: "What is our dispute among ourselves?" Then when ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, was killed, they said: "This is our dispute among ourselves."

It was also said: Their disputing is their being brought to judgment before Allah the Exalted, so that He takes from the good deeds of the oppressor according to the measure of his injustice, and returns them to the good deeds of the one to whom the right was due. This is general concerning all injustices, as in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you know who the bankrupt is?" They said: "The bankrupt among us is one who has no dirham and no property." He said: "Indeed, the bankrupt of my Ummah is one who comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting and zakat, but comes having reviled this one, slandered that one, consumed the property of this one, shed the blood of this one, and beaten this one. So this one is given from his good deeds, and that one from his good deeds. If his good deeds are exhausted before he has settled what is upon him, then some of their sins are taken and cast upon him, and then he is thrown into the Fire." Related by Muslim.

The meaning has already been discussed thoroughly in Al ʿImran [see vol. 4, p. of the first or second edition].

In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a wrong against anyone, regarding his honour or anything else, let him seek his pardon for it today, before there is no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, a portion equal to his wrong will be taken from them; and if he has no good deeds, some of the evil deeds of his companion will be taken and laid upon him."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 32–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah﴾, meaning: there is no one more unjust than one who lies about Allah, claiming that He has a son and a partner, ﴿and denies the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ The interrogative here is for affirmation (istifham taqrir). ﴿Mathwa﴾ means a place of residence for those who deny, and it is derived from thawa bi-l-makan, when one stays in a place: yathwi thawa'an and thuwiyyan, like mada, mada'an and mudiyyan. If it were from athwa, it would have been mathwan. This indicates that thawa is the eloquent dialect. Abu 'Ubayd related athwa and recited the verse of al-A'sha:

Athwa wa-qassara laylatan li-yazawwada... wa-madha wa-akhlafa min Qutaylata mawʻadan

Al-Asma'i knew only thawa and would narrate the verse as athawa, in the interrogative form. Athwaytu ghayri is transitive, and it is also used intransitively.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it﴾ is in the position of raf' as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾. There has been disagreement about "the one who brings the truth and confirms it." Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "the one who brings the truth" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and "confirms it" is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Mujahid said: the Prophet, peace be upon him, and Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Suddi said: "the one who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "the one who confirms it" is Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and Qatadah said: "the one who brings the truth" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and "confirms it" refers to the believers. They based this on His saying, ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾, just as He said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: "the one who brings the truth and confirms it" refers to the believers who will come with the Qur'an on the Day of Resurrection and say: "This is what You gave us; we have followed what is in it." Thus "alladhi" in this case carries the meaning of the plural, just as "man" can carry the meaning of the plural. It was also said: rather, the letter nun has been dropped from it because of the length of the name. al-Sha'bi interpreted it as singular and said: "the one who brings the truth" is Muhammad (ﷺ), so its predicate here is plural, as one says of someone who is honoured: "they did" and "Zayd did such and such." It was also said: this is general for everyone who calls to the Oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, and al-Tabari chose it. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "and those who brought the truth and confirmed it" (wa-alladhina ja'u bi-l-sidqi wa-saddaqu bihi), which is a recitation by way of explanation. In the recitation of Abu Salih al-Kufi: "wa-alladhi ja'a bi-l-sidqi wa-sadaqa bihi" with a light pronunciation, meaning "and confirmed by His coming with it," that is, he was truthful in obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The discussion of "alladhi" has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 212, second or third edition.]], and that it can be singular or plural. ﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, meaning of bliss in Paradise, as one says: "You have honour with me," meaning that such things will reach you from me. ﴿That is the reward of the good-doers﴾: praise in this world and reward in the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that Allah may expiate from them﴾, meaning: those who confirmed it, ﴿so that Allah may expiate from them﴾. ﴿The worst of what they did﴾, meaning: He will honour them and not hold them to account for what they did before Islam. ﴿And reward them their wage﴾, meaning: He will reward them for the acts of obedience in this world ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, which is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 32–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah﴾, meaning: there is no one more unjust than one who lies about Allah, claiming that He has a son and a partner, ﴿and denies the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ The interrogative here is for affirmation (istifham taqrir). ﴿Mathwa﴾ means a place of residence for those who deny, and it is derived from thawa bi-l-makan, when one stays in a place: yathwi thawa'an and thuwiyyan, like mada, mada'an and mudiyyan. If it were from athwa, it would have been mathwan. This indicates that thawa is the eloquent dialect. Abu 'Ubayd related athwa and recited the verse of al-A'sha:

Athwa wa-qassara laylatan li-yazawwada... wa-madha wa-akhlafa min Qutaylata mawʻadan

Al-Asma'i knew only thawa and would narrate the verse as athawa, in the interrogative form. Athwaytu ghayri is transitive, and it is also used intransitively.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it﴾ is in the position of raf' as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾. There has been disagreement about "the one who brings the truth and confirms it." Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "the one who brings the truth" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and "confirms it" is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Mujahid said: the Prophet, peace be upon him, and Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Suddi said: "the one who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "the one who confirms it" is Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and Qatadah said: "the one who brings the truth" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and "confirms it" refers to the believers. They based this on His saying, ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾, just as He said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: "the one who brings the truth and confirms it" refers to the believers who will come with the Qur'an on the Day of Resurrection and say: "This is what You gave us; we have followed what is in it." Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 36–37:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The yā' has been dropped from "kāfin" because it is quiescent and the tanwīn after it is quiescent. The original form would be not to drop it in pausal reading, since the tanwīn has gone, but it has been dropped so that it is known that it is so in continuous reading (waṣl). Among the Arabs there are those who retain it in pausal reading according to the original form, saying "kāfī." The reading of the majority is "ʿabdahu" in the singular, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ): Allah suffices him against the threats and plots of the polytheists. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "ʿibādahu" (His servants), meaning the prophets, or the prophets and the believers who follow them. Abū ʿUbayd chose the reading of the majority because of His saying immediately after it: ﴿And they frighten you with those besides Him.﴾ It is possible that "ʿabd" is a generic noun, like His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 2]. On this view, the first reading returns to the second. "Al-kifāyah" (sufficiency) is the evil of the idols, for they used to frighten the believers with the idols, until Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 81]. Al-Jurjani said: Allah suffices His servant, the believer, and His servant, the disbeliever; the former with reward and the latter with punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they frighten you with those besides Him.﴾ This is because they threatened the Prophet (ﷺ) with the harm of the idols, saying: "Do you revile our gods? If you do not desist from mentioning them, they will surely drive you mad or afflict you with harm." Qatadah said: Khalid ibn al-Walid went to al-ʿUzzā to break it with an axe. Its custodian (sādin) said to him: "I warn you of it, O Khalid, for it has a power that nothing can withstand." Khalid then made for al-ʿUzzā and smashed its nose until he broke it with the axe. Their frightening Khalid is a frightening of the Prophet (ﷺ), because it was he who had directed Khalid. The verse also includes their frightening the Prophet (ﷺ) with the multitude of their numbers and their strength, as He said: ﴿Or do they say, "We are a victorious host"?﴾ [al-Qamar: 44]. "And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide" has already passed. "And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah Mighty, Owner of Retribution?" That is: against whoever opposes Him or opposes His messengers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 38–41:

Allah's statement: ﴿And if you asked them﴾, meaning: and if you asked them, O Muhammad, ﴿"Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ He makes clear that they, despite their worship of idols, acknowledge that the Creator is Allah. Since Allah is the Creator, how can they frighten you with their gods, which are created by Allah the Exalted, when you are the Messenger of Allah, who created them and created the heavens and the earth?

﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾ meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, after their acknowledgement of this, ﴿"Have you considered?" If Allah intends for me harm,﴾ that is, hardship and affliction, ﴿are they the ones who could remove His harm?﴾ meaning these idols; ﴿or if He intends for me mercy,﴾ blessing and ease, ﴿are they the ones who could withhold His mercy?﴾

Muqatil said: The Prophet ﷺ asked them, and they fell silent. Others said: They said, "It does not repel anything that Allah has decreed, but it intercedes." So it was revealed: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me."﴾ He omitted the answer, as the context indicates it, meaning: they would say, "No" (that is, they neither remove nor withhold). [[The addition is from the marginal notes of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi.]] So say, [you,] ﴿"Allah is sufficient for me." In Him I have put my trust,﴾ that is, I have relied upon Him, ﴿and in Him the trusting put their trust,﴾ meaning those who rely place their reliance. The discussion of trust (tawakkul) has already been presented. [[See vol. 4, pp. 189 and 253, first or second edition.]]

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and the Kufans, except 'Asim, read ﴿kashifatu darrihi﴾ with tanwin. Abu 'Amr, Shu'bah, and what is well known from the recitation of al-Hasan and 'Asim read ﴿hal hunna kashifatu durrihi﴾ (without tanwin, in the annexed form).

﴿mumsikatu rahmatihi﴾ with tanwin is the original form, and it is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because it is an active participle with future meaning; and when it is so, the tanwin is better. The poet said:

*The ones who strike 'Umayr away from their homes, and by night, on the day when 'Umayr is an unjust transgressor.*

Had it been in the past tense, tanwin would not be permitted. Omitting the tanwin is according to the strict usage, and when you omit the tanwin, there remains no barrier between the two nouns, so you put the second in the genitive by annexation. Omitting the tanwin is common and well attested in Arabic speech. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [hadyan baligha al-ka'bah], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ [inna mursilu al-naqah]. Sibawayh said: Similar to that is ﴿not violating the game﴾ [ghayra muhillي al-sayd]. Sibawayh recited:

*Are you sending a dinar for our need, or 'Abd Rabb, brother of 'Awn ibn Mikhraq?*

And al-Nabighah said:

*Judge as the wisdom of the girl of the tribe when she looked, and at a pigeon, a swift-flying one, coming to the scant water.* [[The poet is addressing al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, who was displeased with him: be wise in my affair as the wisdom of Zarqa' al-Yamamah in estimating the pigeons that passed by her flying. Her story is well known. The shara' is the place from which one descends to the water, and the thamd is the little water on the surface of the ground.]]

Its meaning is "coming to the scant water," so the tanwin is omitted, like ﴿kashifatu darrihi﴾.

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. So you will soon know.﴾ meaning: according to my position, that is, according to my way which is established with me, ﴿"so you will soon know."﴾ Abu Bakr read ﴿makanatikum﴾ in the plural. This has already been discussed in al-An'am. [[See vol. 7, p. 89, first or second edition.]]

﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, meaning it will humiliate and abase him, that is in this world, and that is by hunger and the sword. ﴿And upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own soul; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it. And you are not over them a manager.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been presented fully in other places. [[See vol. 8, pp. 388 onward, first or second edition.]]
