*Judge as the wisdom of the girl of the tribe when she looked, and at a pigeon, a swift-flying one, coming to the scant water.* [[The poet is addressing al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, who was displeased with him: be wise in my affair as the wisdom of Zarqa' al-Yamamah in estimating the pigeons that passed by her flying. Her story is well known. The shara' is the place from which one descends to the water, and the thamd is the little water on the surface of the ground.]]

Its meaning is "coming to the scant water," so the tanwin is omitted, like ﴿kashifatu darrihi﴾.

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. So you will soon know.﴾ meaning: according to my position, that is, according to my way which is established with me, ﴿"so you will soon know."﴾ Abu Bakr read ﴿makanatikum﴾ in the plural. This has already been discussed in al-An'am. [[See vol. 7, p. 89, first or second edition.]]

﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, meaning it will humiliate and abase him, that is in this world, and that is by hunger and the sword. ﴿And upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own soul; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it. And you are not over them a manager.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been presented fully in other places. [[See vol. 8, pp. 388 onward, first or second edition.]]

There are four issues in this passage.

The first: Allah's words, ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, meaning He seizes them when their terms come to an end. "And those that do not die during their sleep": scholars differ on this. It has been said that He withdraws them from acting while their spirits remain in their bodies, "so He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back" (﴿He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back﴾), meaning the sleepers, and He releases them to act until the time of their death. Ibn Isa [[In one copy: Abu Isa said it.]] said this. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that He seizes those that do not die during their sleep when their term is complete. He said: their taking (tawaffi) may be their sleep, so the sense on this view is "and those whose taking is their sleep." Ibn Abbas and other exegetes said: the spirits of the living and the dead meet in sleep and know one another as much as Allah wills. When He wills to return all of them to their bodies, He holds the spirits of the dead with Him and releases the spirits of the living to their bodies. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Allah seizes the spirits of the dead when they die and the spirits of the living when they sleep, and they become acquainted as much as Allah wills. "He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back," meaning He returns them. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: whatever the soul of the sleeper sees while it is in the sky, before it is sent back to its body, is a true vision; and whatever it sees after being sent back and before settling in its body is what the devils cast into it, and they make falsehoods appear to it, and that is a false vision.

Ibn Zayd said: sleep is a taking and death is a taking. The Prophet ﷺ said: "As you sleep, so you die, and as you are woken, so you are raised." Umar said: sleep is the brother of death. It is also transmitted as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah: it was said, "O Messenger of Allah, do the people of Paradise sleep?" He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Al-Daraqutni recorded it. Ibn Abbas said: "In the son of Adam there is a nafs (soul) and a ruh (spirit), between them like the ray of the sun. The nafs is that by which there is reason and discernment, and the ruh is that by which there is breath and movement. When the servant sleeps, Allah seizes his nafs but does not seize his ruh." This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari and al-Zajjaj. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: this is far-fetched, since the apparent meaning of the verse is that the soul taken in both states is one thing. This is why He said, "He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back until an appointed term." So Allah takes the spirit in two states: in the state of sleep and in the state of death. What He takes in sleep means that He covers it with what restrains it from acting, so it is as if it were held. What He takes in death, He keeps and does not release until the Day of Resurrection. His words "and sends the others back" mean He removes what restrains it, and it returns as it was. So the taking of souls in sleep is by removing sensation and creating heedlessness and a defect in the place of perception, and their taking in death is by creating death and completely removing sensation. "He keeps those for which He has decreed death," by not creating perception in them, since He has created death in them. "And sends the others back," by returning sensation to them.

Second issue: scholars have differed over this verse concerning the nafs and the ruh, whether they are one thing or two, as we have mentioned. The more evident view is that they are one thing, and this is what the sound reports indicate, as we will mention in this chapter. Among them is the hadith of Umm Salama, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon Abu Salama when his eye had been opened [[Shaqqa basaruhu: meaning it had opened.]], so he closed it and said: "When the ruh is seized, the sight follows it." Also the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you not see that when a person dies his gaze becomes fixed?" He said: "That is when his gaze follows his nafs." Muslim recorded both. He also reported from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The angels attend, and if the man is righteous they say: 'Come out, O good nafs, that were in a good body. Come out praised, and rejoice in mercy, fragrance, and a Lord who is pleased, not angry.' It continues to be said to it until it comes out, and then it is raised to the sky." He mentioned the hadith, and its chain is sound. Ibn Majah recorded it, and we have mentioned it in al-Tadhkira. In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra: "When the ruh of the believer departs, two angels meet it and ascend with it." He mentioned the hadith. Bilal, in the hadith of the valley, said: "O Messenger of Allah, He who took my nafs has taken your nafs." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, responding to him in the hadith of Zayd ibn Aslam about the valley: "O people, Allah has seized our spirits, and if He willed He would have returned them to us at a time other than this."

Third issue: the correct view concerning it is that it is a subtle body, interlaced with perceptible bodies. It is drawn out and removed, it is wrapped and folded in its shroud, and with it one is raised to the sky. It does not die and does not perish. It is among things that have a beginning but no end. It has two eyes and two hands, and it has a pleasant and a foul smell, as in the hadith of Abu Hurayra. This is the description of bodies, not of accidents. We have mentioned all these reports in the book al-Tadhkira, concerning the conditions of the dead and the matters of the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 83], meaning the nafs until its departure from the body, and this is a description of a body. And Allah knows best.

Fourth issue: al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you goes to his bed, let him take the inner edge of his waist-wrap and shake his bed with it, and let him mention the name of Allah, for he does not know what came upon his bed after him. When he wants to lie down, let him lie on his right side and say: 'Glory be to You, my Lord, I have laid my side down and by You I raise it. If You take my nafs, then forgive it; and if You send it back, then protect it with what You protect Your righteous servants with.'" Al-Bukhari, Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi said "then have mercy on it" instead of "then forgive it." Al-Tirmidhi added: "And when he wakes, let him say: 'Praise be to Allah who has given me health in my body, returned my ruh to me, and permitted me to remember Him.'" Al-Bukhari recorded from Hudhayfa, who said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took his bed at night, he placed his hand under his cheek and then said: "O Allah, in Your name I die and I live." When he woke, he said: "Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection."

His words, ﴿He keeps those for which He has decreed death﴾: this is the recitation of the majority, with the verb in the active form, the word "death" (al-mawt) in the accusative. The meaning is that Allah decreed death for them. This is the preference of Abu Hatim and Abu Ubayd, because of His words at the beginning of the verse, "Allah takes the souls," so He is the one who decrees over them. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited qudiya alayha al-mawtu (passive voice, where the agent is not named). Al-Nahhas said: the meaning is the same, except that the first recitation is clearer and more consistent with the structure of the speech, because they have all agreed on "and sends," and none recited "and is sent" (wa yursal).

In the verse there is a reminder of His great power and of His being singular in divinity, and that He does what He wills, gives life and causes death, and none other than Him is able to do this. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, meaning in Allah's seizing the soul of the dead and the sleeper, and His sending back the soul of the sleeper and withholding the soul of the dead, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾.

Al-Asma'i said: I heard Mu'tamir say: the spirit of a human is like a ball of spun thread. The spirit is sent out, and it goes, then it goes, then it is folded and comes back and enters. So the meaning of the verse is that some of the spirit is sent out during sleep, while most of it remains in the body, connected to what has gone out of it by a subtle connection. When the person wakes, most of his spirit pulls back what has extended from it, and it returns. Other views have been stated. In the revelation: ﴿They ask you about the ruh. Say: The ruh is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85], meaning that none knows its reality except Allah. This has been discussed earlier in [Surat Subhan [[See vol. 1, p. 323 and following, edition one or two.]]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 43–45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ That is, "Rather, they have taken," meaning the idols. In the speech there is something implying "not": that is, "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect" (they did not reflect), but rather they took their gods as intercessors. ﴿Say: Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾ That is, say to them, O Muhammad: Do you take them as intercessors even though they possess nothing of intercession and do not understand, because they are inanimate objects? This is a rhetorical question of denial. ﴿Say: To Allah belongs all intercession.﴾ This is explicit that intercession belongs to Allah alone, as He said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], so there is no intercessor except by His allowance, ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. "Jami'an" (all) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). If it is said: "jami'an" is only used for two or more, while intercession is singular? The answer: intercession is a verbal noun (masdar), and a verbal noun can stand for the dual and the plural. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; then to Him you will be returned.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and as a circumstantial state according to Yunus. "Ishma'azzat" (were constricted): al-Mubarrad said: they contracted. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Qatadah said: they recoiled, became arrogant, disbelieved and became defiant. Al-Mu'arrij said: they denied. The root meaning of al-ishmi'zaz is aversion and turning away. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"When the spear-shaft bites into them, they recoil, and it turns them away, a hard, unyielding, repelling (lance)" [The thiqaf is what spears are straightened with; 'ashwazanah means hard and very firm; zabun means one that pushes away. The verse describes a lance, and before it is:

"Indeed our lance, O 'Amr, has refused, against the enemies before you, to be softened."]

Abu Zayd said: "ishma'azza al-rajul" means he was frightened by a terror, and he is one who is terrified. When it was said to the polytheists, "There is no god but Allah," they recoiled and disbelieved. ﴿And when those besides Him are mentioned﴾ meaning the idols, at the time when Satan cast into the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited Surah [al-Najm], those "high cranes" (al-gharaniq al-ula), and that their intercession is to be hoped for. [See what has been said about this statement, its contradiction of infallibility, and the interpretations of His saying in Surah al-Hajj: "We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire" (vol. 12, p. 79 and following).] This was said by a group of exegetes. ﴿Then they rejoice﴾ meaning joy and happiness appear in their faces.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 46–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾ The word ﴿اللَّهُمَّ﴾ is in the accusative (nasb) because it is a vocative (nida' (direct address)) followed by an annexed noun, and likewise ﴿عَالِمَ الْغَيْبِ﴾. According to Sibawayh, it is not permissible for it to be a qualifier (na't (adjective)). "You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing." In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, who said: I asked A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): With what did the Prophet (ﷺ) begin his prayer when he stood up at night? She said: When he stood at night, he would open his prayer with: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il," and Israfil, "Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing. Guide me to the truth in what has been disputed, by Your permission, for You guide whom You will to a straight path."

"When the news of the killing of al-Husayn ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) reached al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, he recited: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Indeed, I know a verse that no one has ever recited while asking Allah for something without Him giving it to him: His saying, ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved and associated partners with Allah. ﴿From the evil of the punishment﴾, meaning from the evil of the punishment of that Day. This has passed in surah "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 131, first or second edition.]] and "al-Ra'd" [[See vol. 9, p. 307, first or second edition.]].

﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾. Among the most notable reports on this is what Mansur narrated from Mujahid, who said: They did deeds that they supposed were good deeds, but they were evil deeds. As-Suddi also said this. It was also said: They did deeds that they supposed they would repent from before death, but death overtook them before they repented, while they had thought they would be saved by repentance. It is also possible that they supposed that He would forgive them without repentance. So ﴿there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾ refers to entering the Fire. Sufyan al-Thawri said regarding this verse: Woe to the people of showing off (riya'), woe to the people of showing off; this is their verse and their story. Ikrimah ibn Ammar said: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir showed intense anguish at his death. It was said to him: Why this anguish? He said: I fear a verse from the Book of Allah: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾, so I fear that there will appear to me what I had not been expecting.

﴿And there will appear to them﴾, meaning it becomes manifest to them, ﴿the evils of what they earned﴾, meaning the punishment for what they earned of disbelief and disobedience. ﴿And there will surround them﴾, meaning it encompasses them and descends upon them, ﴿that at which they used to mock.﴾

"When the news of the killing of al-Husayn ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) reached al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, he recited: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Indeed, I know a verse that no one has ever recited while asking Allah for something without Him giving it to him: His saying, ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved and associated partners with Allah. ﴿From the evil of the punishment﴾, meaning from the evil of the punishment of that Day. This has passed in surah "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 131, first or second edition.]] and "al-Ra'd" [[See vol. 9, p. 307, first or second edition.]].

﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾. Among the most notable reports on this is what Mansur narrated from Mujahid, who said: They did deeds that they supposed were good deeds, but they were evil deeds. As-Suddi also said this. It was also said: They did deeds that they supposed they would repent from before death, but death overtook them before they repented, while they had thought they would be saved by repentance. It is also possible that they supposed that He would forgive them without repentance. So ﴿there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾ refers to entering the Fire. Sufyan al-Thawri said regarding this verse: Woe to the people of showing off (riya'), woe to the people of showing off; this is their verse and their story. Ikrimah ibn Ammar said: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir showed intense anguish at his death. It was said to him: Why this anguish? He said: I fear a verse from the Book of Allah: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting﴾, so I fear that there will appear to me what I had not been expecting.

﴿And there will appear to them﴾, meaning it becomes manifest to them, ﴿the evils of what they earned﴾, meaning the punishment for what they earned of disbelief and disobedience. ﴿And there will surround them﴾, meaning it encompasses them and descends upon them, ﴿that at which they used to mock.﴾

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 49–52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah.

"Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us, he says, 'I was only given it because of knowledge.'" Qatadah said: "because of knowledge" means, "with my knowledge of the ways of gaining wealth." It is also narrated from him: "because of knowledge" means "because of the good that is with me." It was said: "because of knowledge" means "because of knowledge from Allah regarding my merit." Al-Hasan said: "because of knowledge" means "by knowledge that Allah taught me." It was also said: the meaning is that he said, "I know that if I am given this in the world, I have a standing with Allah." "Allah said: 'Rather, it is a trial'," meaning: rather, the favours you have been given are a trial by which you are tested. Al-Farra' said: He made "it" feminine because of the feminine gender of "fitnah" (trial); had he said "rather, it is a trial (huwa fitnatun)" it would have been permissible. Al-Nahhas said: the implied sense is "rather, I gave him a trial." "But most of them do not know," meaning they do not know that the giving of wealth to them is a test.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those before them had already said it﴾. It is feminine in agreement with the feminine gender of the word (kalimah). "Those who came before them," meaning the disbelievers before them, such as Qarun and others, who said: "I was only given it because of knowledge with me." "So what they had earned did not avail them," "ma" here is for negation, meaning their wealth and their children did not avail them anything against the punishment of Allah. It was also said: meaning, "what then availed their wealth?" and "innama" is then interrogative. "So the evil consequences of what they had earned struck them," meaning the recompense for the evil of their deeds. The recompense of an evil deed is sometimes also called an evil deed. "And those who did wrong," meaning those who associated partners with Allah, "from among these people," not from the (other) nation, "the evil consequences of what they earned will strike them," meaning by famine and the sword. "And they will not escape," meaning they will not outrun Allah or escape Him. This has already been discussed [see vol. 7, p. 88, first or second edition, and vol. 8, p. 351, first or second edition].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. He specified the believer for mention, because he is the one who reflects upon the signs and benefits from them, and he knows that abundance of provision may be a deception and a gradual leading astray (istidraj), while its restriction may be an elevation and a magnification.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 53–59 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾. It is permissible to delete the yā' (the final ya of "ʿibādī"), because the vocative is a place of deletion. Al-Naḥḥās (a grammarian and exegete) said: Among the most excellent reports concerning it is that of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUmar, who said: When we gathered for the emigration (hijrah), I, Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī, and ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah ibn ʿUtbah agreed upon a meeting place, the ʾAḍāh (a pond) of the Banū Ghifār. We said: Whoever is delayed among us has been detained, so let his companion proceed. I and ʿAyyāsh ibn ʿUtbah arrived in the morning, but Hishām was detained from us, and then he was tested and succumbed to the test. We used to say in Medina: These people knew God, the Mighty and Majestic, and believed in His Messenger (ﷺ), then they fell into trial because of a calamity that befell them; we do not see any repentance for them. They, too, were saying this to themselves. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed in His Book: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God," up to His saying, may He be exalted: "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" ʿUmar said: So I wrote it with my own hand and sent it to Hishām. Hishām said: When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhū Ṭuwā and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us, so I returned, sat upon my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

And from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A group of the polytheists had killed much and committed fornication much, and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), or sent to him: "What you call to is good, but do you inform us that there is repentance for us?" So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves." Al-Bukhārī related it in meaning.

It has already passed at the end of al-Furqān (vol. 13, p. 76 ff., first or second edition).

And from Ibn ʿAbbās also: It was revealed concerning the people of Mecca, who said: "Muḥammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul which God has forbidden will not be forgiven. How can we emigrate and submit, when we have worshipped another god along with God and killed the soul which God has forbidden?" So God revealed this verse.

It is said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had transgressed against themselves in worship and feared that it would not be accepted from them because of sins they had committed in the pre-Islamic period (al-jāhiliyyah).

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and ʿAṭāʾ (said): It was revealed concerning Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamzah, because he thought that God would not accept his Islam. Ibn Jurayj related from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Waḥshī came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muḥammad, I have come to you seeking protection, so grant me protection until I hear the speech of God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I had wished to see you without a pact of protection. But since you have come to me seeking protection, you are under my protection until you hear the speech of God." He said: "Indeed I have associated others with God, I have killed the soul which God has forbidden, and I have committed fornication. Will God accept repentance from me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent until there was revealed: "And those who do not invoke with God another god, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, nor commit fornication" [al-Furqān: 68], up to the end of the verse. He recited it to him. He said: "I see a condition. Perhaps I will not do righteous deeds. I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 48]. He summoned him and recited it to him. He said: "Perhaps I am among those whom He does not will (to forgive). I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." He said: "Yes, now I see no condition," and he embraced Islam.

Ḥammād ibn Salamah related from Thābit, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Asmāʾ that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd: "Indeed God forgives all sins, for whomever He wills."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: These two readings are by way of explanation, i.e., God forgives whomever He wills. God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows whom He wills to forgive, namely the penitent, or one who committed a minor sin and had no major sin. This indicates that He intends the penitent by what follows: "And turn in repentance to your Lord." So the penitent has all his sins forgiven. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 82]. This is without difficulty.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: There is no verse in the Qur'an broader in scope than this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." This has already passed in (sūrat) Subḥān (vol. 1, p. 322 ff., first or second edition).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās refuted them and said: The most hopeful verse in the Qur'an is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. This has passed in (sūrat) al-Raʿd (vol. 9, p. 285, first or second edition).

It is read "wa-lā taqnaṭū" with kasrah and with fatḥah on the nūn. Its explanation has passed in (sūrat) al-Ḥijr (vol. 10, p. 36, first or second edition).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾, i.e., return to Him in obedience. When He explained that whoever repents from polytheism will be forgiven, He commanded repentance and return to Him. Inābah (turning in repentance) is returning to God with sincerity.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, i.e., humble yourselves before Him and obey Him, ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ in this world, ﴿then you will not be helped﴾, i.e., you will not be prevented from His punishment. It is related in a ḥadīth from Jābir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among happiness is that God lengthens a person's life in obedience and grants him inābah, and indeed among wretchedness is that a person does deeds and is pleased with his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. "The best of what was sent down" is the Qur'an, and all of it is good. The meaning, as al-Ḥasan said: Adhere to His obedience and avoid His disobedience. Al-Suddī said: The best is what God commanded in His Book. Ibn Zayd said: That is, the clear (muḥkam) verses, and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābih) to its knower. He said: God sent down books, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms, then He sent down the Qur'an and commanded following it, so it is the best and it is the inimitable (muʿjiz). It was also said: This is the best because it abrogates and supersedes all the books, while all the books are abrogated. It was said: It means pardon, because God gave His Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice between pardon and retaliation. It was said: What God taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) that is not Qur'an is good, and what was revealed to him of the Qur'an is the best. It was said: The best of what was sent down to you is the reports of the past nations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me"﴾. The "an" (lest) is in the accusative position, meaning "out of dislike that a soul should say." According to the Kufans it means "so that it does not say," and according to the Basrans it means "for fear that it says." It was said: That is, "lest a soul say," because He said before this: "before the punishment comes upon you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why is "nafs" indefinite? I say: Because what is meant by it is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that it means a soul distinguished from the (other) souls, either by intense obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that it means multiplicity, as al-Aʿshā said:

"And many a open space, if I shouted in its air, a noble man would come to me shaking his head in anger."

He means groups of nobles who would help him, not a single noble, and its parallel is: "Many a land have I crossed, and many a champion have I fought," where only multiplicity is intended.

"Yā ḥasratā": the original is "yā ḥasratī," and the yā' was replaced by an alif, because it is lighter and more suited to prolonging the voice in calling out (istighāthah). They sometimes attach a hā' to it. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O welcome, O donkey that is swift..." (al-Nājiyah: swift; in al-Farrāʾ's tafsīr it is "nāhiyah" instead of "nājiyah," and so it is related in al-Lisān and Sharḥ al-Qāmūs under the root sanā. Here al-sāniyah is a verbal noun on the pattern fāʿilah meaning irrigation; he meant his water-skin for irrigating.)
"When he comes, I bring him near to the irrigating (camel)."

They sometimes attach a yā' after the alif to indicate possession, and thus Abū Jaʿfar recited it: "Yā ḥasratāy." And ḥasrah means regret.

﴿Over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: In obedience to God. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That is, in the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He said: That is, the Qur'an and acting upon it. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "In God's side" means in God's reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: The janb (side) is nearness and proximity. It is said: "So-and-so lives in the side of so-and-so," meaning in his neighborhood, and from it is "and the companion at the side" (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb), meaning: over what I neglected in seeking His neighborhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, over the path which is God's path, to which He called me. The Arabs call the cause and the path to a thing a janb. They say: "I swallowed sorrows in your side," meaning for your sake, because of you, and for the sake of your pleasure. It was also said: "In God's side" means in the direction that leads to God's pleasure and reward. The Arabs call a direction janb. The poet said:

"The heart was divided, striving for that: the people are a side, and the commander is a side."

Meaning the people from one side and the commander from another side. Ibn ʿArafah said: That is, I abandoned God's command. It is said: "I did not do that in the side of my need," meaning... Kuthayyir said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a lover, who has a heart burning for you, torn to pieces?"

Mujāhid also said likewise, meaning: I wasted some of God's command. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man sits in a sitting, nor walks a walk, nor lies down in a place, in which he does not remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it will be a tirah (a loss/burden) upon him on the Day of Resurrection," that is, a ḥasrah [Ibn al-Athīr explained it in al-Nihāyah as deficiency or liability]. Abū Dāwūd related it in meaning.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: Among the regrets of the Day of Resurrection is that a man sees his wealth, which God gave him in this world, on the Day of Resurrection in the scale of another, who inherited it and acted with it in truth, so he has its reward and the other has its burden. Among the regrets is that a man sees his slave, whom God placed under his authority in this world, nearer in rank to God, the Mighty and Majestic, or sees a man whom he knew blind in this world, now seeing on the Day of Resurrection while he himself is blind.

﴿And indeed I was among the scoffers﴾, i.e., I was only among those who mocked the Qur'an and the Messenger in this world, and the friends of God. Qatādah said: It was not enough for him that he neglected obedience to God, until he mocked its people. The place of "in kuntu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he said: "I neglected while I was mocking," i.e., I neglected in the state of my mockery. It was also said: I was only in mockery, play, and falsehood, i.e., my striving was only in the worship of other than God, the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿"If only God had guided me"﴾, i.e., had shown me the way to His religion, ﴿"I would have been among the righteous"﴾, i.e., among those who avoid polytheism and sins. This saying, "If only God had guided me, I would have been guided," is a true statement, though it is close to the argument of the polytheists about which the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, informed concerning them in His saying: "Those who associated will say: 'If God had willed, we would not have associated.'" So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

Then he put it in the accusative (naṣb). (تُسْئَلُ) is in the accusative because it agrees in position with الذكرى (remembrance), since the meaning of the sentence is: "What is it to you from it but that you remember," as in the saying: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," meaning: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," i.e., "Would that I wore a cloak and was cool."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do acts of disobedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of a man of the people of Paradise, so he enters Paradise." He said, "Why should I tire myself?" So he abandoned his deeds and took to wickedness and disobedience. Iblis said to him, "You have a long life, so enjoy the world, then repent." So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." It is as if this speaker had said, "I was not guided," so it was said, "Yes indeed, the path of guidance was made clear to you, and you were in a position where, had you wished to believe, you would have been able to believe."

"My signs" means the Qur'an. It is also said that by "the signs" are meant the miracles, i.e., the proof was clear, but you denied it and rejected it, (and you were arrogant), meaning you were too proud to believe, (and were among the disbelievers).

He said "you were arrogant and you were" in the masculine address, because the word nafs (soul/self) applies to both male and female. It is said: "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Al-Mubarrad said: The Arabs say "nafs wāḥid," meaning one person.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited: "Indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers."

Al-A'mash recited: "Bala, qad jā'athu āyātī" (in the third person), and this indicates the sense of remembrance. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas did not meet Umm Salamah, but the recitation (qirā'ah) is permissible, because nafs can apply to both masculine and feminine. Some have rejected this recitation and said: If the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra, then one must say: "wa kunti min al-kawāfir" or "min al-kāfirāt." Al-Nahhas said: This does not necessarily follow. Do you not see that before it there is: "lest a soul should say," then he said: "wa in kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn," and he did not say "min al-sawākhir" or "min al-sākhirāt." The rule in Arabic is that the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra in "wa istakbarta wa kunta" (you were arrogant and you were), which is from the plural "al-sākhirīn," or "min al-nās al-sākhirīn," or "min al-qawm al-sākhirīn."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 53–59 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾. It is permissible to delete the yā' (the final ya of "ʿibādī"), because the vocative is a place of deletion. Al-Naḥḥās (a grammarian and exegete) said: Among the most excellent reports concerning it is that of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUmar, who said: When we gathered for the emigration (hijrah), I, Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī, and ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah ibn ʿUtbah agreed upon a meeting place, the ʾAḍāh (a pond) of the Banū Ghifār. We said: Whoever is delayed among us has been detained, so let his companion proceed. I and ʿAyyāsh ibn ʿUtbah arrived in the morning, but Hishām was detained from us, and then he was tested and succumbed to the test. We used to say in Medina: These people knew God, the Mighty and Majestic, and believed in His Messenger (ﷺ), then they fell into trial because of a calamity that befell them; we do not see any repentance for them. They, too, were saying this to themselves. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed in His Book: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God," up to His saying, may He be exalted: "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" ʿUmar said: So I wrote it with my own hand and sent it to Hishām. Hishām said: When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhū Ṭuwā and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us, so I returned, sat upon my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

And from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A group of the polytheists had killed much and committed fornication much, and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), or sent to him: "What you call to is good, but do you inform us that there is repentance for us?" So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves." Al-Bukhārī related it in meaning.

It has already passed at the end of al-Furqān (vol. 13, p. 76 ff., first or second edition).

And from Ibn ʿAbbās also: It was revealed concerning the people of Mecca, who said: "Muḥammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul which God has forbidden will not be forgiven. How can we emigrate and submit, when we have worshipped another god along with God and killed the soul which God has forbidden?" So God revealed this verse.

It is said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had transgressed against themselves in worship and feared that it would not be accepted from them because of sins they had committed in the pre-Islamic period (al-jāhiliyyah).

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and ʿAṭāʾ (said): It was revealed concerning Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamzah, because he thought that God would not accept his Islam. Ibn Jurayj related from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Waḥshī came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muḥammad, I have come to you seeking protection, so grant me protection until I hear the speech of God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I had wished to see you without a pact of protection. But since you have come to me seeking protection, you are under my protection until you hear the speech of God." He said: "Indeed I have associated others with God, I have killed the soul which God has forbidden, and I have committed fornication. Will God accept repentance from me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent until there was revealed: "And those who do not invoke with God another god, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, nor commit fornication" [al-Furqān: 68], up to the end of the verse. He recited it to him. He said: "I see a condition. Perhaps I will not do righteous deeds. I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 48]. He summoned him and recited it to him. He said: "Perhaps I am among those whom He does not will (to forgive). I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." He said: "Yes, now I see no condition," and he embraced Islam.

Ḥammād ibn Salamah related from Thābit, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Asmāʾ that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd: "Indeed God forgives all sins, for whomever He wills."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: These two readings are by way of explanation, i.e., God forgives whomever He wills. God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows whom He wills to forgive, namely the penitent, or one who committed a minor sin and had no major sin. This indicates that He intends the penitent by what follows: "And turn in repentance to your Lord." So the penitent has all his sins forgiven. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 82]. This is without difficulty.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: There is no verse in the Qur'an broader in scope than this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." This has already passed in (sūrat) Subḥān (vol. 1, p. 322 ff., first or second edition).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās refuted them and said: The most hopeful verse in the Qur'an is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. This has passed in (sūrat) al-Raʿd (vol. 9, p. 285, first or second edition).

It is read "wa-lā taqnaṭū" with kasrah and with fatḥah on the nūn. Its explanation has passed in (sūrat) al-Ḥijr (vol. 10, p. 36, first or second edition).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾, i.e., return to Him in obedience. When He explained that whoever repents from polytheism will be forgiven, He commanded repentance and return to Him. Inābah (turning in repentance) is returning to God with sincerity.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, i.e., humble yourselves before Him and obey Him, ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ in this world, ﴿then you will not be helped﴾, i.e., you will not be prevented from His punishment. It is related in a ḥadīth from Jābir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among happiness is that God lengthens a person's life in obedience and grants him inābah, and indeed among wretchedness is that a person does deeds and is pleased with his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. "The best of what was sent down" is the Qur'an, and all of it is good. The meaning, as al-Ḥasan said: Adhere to His obedience and avoid His disobedience. Al-Suddī said: The best is what God commanded in His Book. Ibn Zayd said: That is, the clear (muḥkam) verses, and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābih) to its knower. He said: God sent down books, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms, then He sent down the Qur'an and commanded following it, so it is the best and it is the inimitable (muʿjiz). It was also said: This is the best because it abrogates and supersedes all the books, while all the books are abrogated. It was said: It means pardon, because God gave His Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice between pardon and retaliation. It was said: What God taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) that is not Qur'an is good, and what was revealed to him of the Qur'an is the best. It was said: The best of what was sent down to you is the reports of the past nations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me"﴾. The "an" (lest) is in the accusative position, meaning "out of dislike that a soul should say." According to the Kufans it means "so that it does not say," and according to the Basrans it means "for fear that it says." It was said: That is, "lest a soul say," because He said before this: "before the punishment comes upon you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why is "nafs" indefinite? I say: Because what is meant by it is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that it means a soul distinguished from the (other) souls, either by intense obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that it means multiplicity, as al-Aʿshā said:

"And many a open space, if I shouted in its air, a noble man would come to me shaking his head in anger."

He means groups of nobles who would help him, not a single noble, and its parallel is: "Many a land have I crossed, and many a champion have I fought," where only multiplicity is intended.

"Yā ḥasratā": the original is "yā ḥasratī," and the yā' was replaced by an alif, because it is lighter and more suited to prolonging the voice in calling out (istighāthah). They sometimes attach a hā' to it. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O welcome, O donkey that is swift..." (al-Nājiyah: swift; in al-Farrāʾ's tafsīr it is "nāhiyah" instead of "nājiyah," and so it is related in al-Lisān and Sharḥ al-Qāmūs under the root sanā. Here al-sāniyah is a verbal noun on the pattern fāʿilah meaning irrigation; he meant his water-skin for irrigating.)
"When he comes, I bring him near to the irrigating (camel)."

They sometimes attach a yā' after the alif to indicate possession, and thus Abū Jaʿfar recited it: "Yā ḥasratāy." And ḥasrah means regret.

﴿Over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: In obedience to God. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That is, in the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He said: That is, the Qur'an and acting upon it. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "In God's side" means in God's reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: The janb (side) is nearness and proximity. It is said: "So-and-so lives in the side of so-and-so," meaning in his neighborhood, and from it is "and the companion at the side" (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb), meaning: over what I neglected in seeking His neighborhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, over the path which is God's path, to which He called me. The Arabs call the cause and the path to a thing a janb. They say: "I swallowed sorrows in your side," meaning for your sake, because of you, and for the sake of your pleasure. It was also said: "In God's side" means in the direction that leads to God's pleasure and reward. The Arabs call a direction janb. The poet said:

"The heart was divided, striving for that: the people are a side, and the commander is a side."

Meaning the people from one side and the commander from another side. Ibn ʿArafah said: That is, I abandoned God's command. It is said: "I did not do that in the side of my need," meaning... Kuthayyir said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a lover, who has a heart burning for you, torn to pieces?"

Mujāhid also said likewise, meaning: I wasted some of God's command. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man sits in a sitting, nor walks a walk, nor lies down in a place, in which he does not remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it will be a tirah (a loss/burden) upon him on the Day of Resurrection," that is, a ḥasrah [Ibn al-Athīr explained it in al-Nihāyah as deficiency or liability]. Abū Dāwūd related it in meaning.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: Among the regrets of the Day of Resurrection is that a man sees his wealth, which God gave him in this world, on the Day of Resurrection in the scale of another, who inherited it and acted with it in truth, so he has its reward and the other has its burden. Among the regrets is that a man sees his slave, whom God placed under his authority in this world, nearer in rank to God, the Mighty and Majestic, or sees a man whom he knew blind in this world, now seeing on the Day of Resurrection while he himself is blind.

﴿And indeed I was among the scoffers﴾, i.e., I was only among those who mocked the Qur'an and the Messenger in this world, and the friends of God. Qatādah said: It was not enough for him that he neglected obedience to God, until he mocked its people. The place of "in kuntu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he said: "I neglected while I was mocking," i.e., I neglected in the state of my mockery. It was also said: I was only in mockery, play, and falsehood, i.e., my striving was only in the worship of other than God, the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿"If only God had guided me"﴾, i.e., had shown me the way to His religion, ﴿"I would have been among the righteous"﴾, i.e., among those who avoid polytheism and sins. This saying, "If only God had guided me, I would have been guided," is a true statement, though it is close to the argument of the polytheists about which the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, informed concerning them in His saying: "Those who associated will say: 'If God had willed, we would not have associated.'" So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows whom He wills to forgive, namely the penitent, or one who committed a minor sin and had no major sin. This indicates that He intends the penitent by what follows: "And turn in repentance to your Lord." So the penitent has all his sins forgiven. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 82]. This is without difficulty.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: There is no verse in the Qur'an broader in scope than this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." This has already passed in (sūrat) Subḥān (vol. 1, p. 322 ff., first or second edition).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās refuted them and said: The most hopeful verse in the Qur'an is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. This has passed in (sūrat) al-Raʿd (vol. 9, p. 285, first or second edition).

It is read "wa-lā taqnaṭū" with kasrah and with fatḥah on the nūn. Its explanation has passed in (sūrat) al-Ḥijr (vol. 10, p. 36, first or second edition).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾, i.e., return to Him in obedience. When He explained that whoever repents from polytheism will be forgiven, He commanded repentance and return to Him. Inābah (turning in repentance) is returning to God with sincerity.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, i.e., humble yourselves before Him and obey Him, ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ in this world, ﴿then you will not be helped﴾, i.e., you will not be prevented from His punishment. It is related in a ḥadīth from Jābir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among happiness is that God lengthens a person's life in obedience and grants him inābah, and indeed among wretchedness is that a person does deeds and is pleased with his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. "The best of what was sent down" is the Qur'an, and all of it is good. The meaning, as al-Ḥasan said: Adhere to His obedience and avoid His disobedience. Al-Suddī said: The best is what God commanded in His Book. Ibn Zayd said: That is, the clear (muḥkam) verses, and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābih) to its knower. He said: God sent down books, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms, then He sent down the Qur'an and commanded following it, so it is the best and it is the inimitable (muʿjiz). It was also said: This is the best because it abrogates and supersedes all the books, while all the books are abrogated. It was said: It means pardon, because God gave His Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice between pardon and retaliation. It was said: What God taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) that is not Qur'an is good, and what was revealed to him of the Qur'an is the best. It was said: The best of what was sent down to you is the reports of the past nations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me"﴾. The "an" (lest) is in the accusative position, meaning "out of dislike that a soul should say." According to the Kufans it means "so that it does not say," and according to the Basrans it means "for fear that it says." It was said: That is, "lest a soul say," because He said before this: "before the punishment comes upon you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why is "nafs" indefinite? I say: Because what is meant by it is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that it means a soul distinguished from the (other) souls, either by intense obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that it means multiplicity, as al-Aʿshā said:

"And many a open space, if I shouted in its air, a noble man would come to me shaking his head in anger."

He means groups of nobles who would help him, not a single noble, and its parallel is: "Many a land have I crossed, and many a champion have I fought," where only multiplicity is intended.

"Yā ḥasratā": the original is "yā ḥasratī," and the yā' was replaced by an alif, because it is lighter and more suited to prolonging the voice in calling out (istighāthah). They sometimes attach a hā' to it. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O welcome, O donkey that is swift..." (al-Nājiyah: swift; in al-Farrāʾ's tafsīr it is "nāhiyah" instead of "nājiyah," and so it is related in al-Lisān and Sharḥ al-Qāmūs under the root sanā. Here al-sāniyah is a verbal noun on the pattern fāʿilah meaning irrigation; he meant his water-skin for irrigating.)
"When he comes, I bring him near to the irrigating (camel)."

They sometimes attach a yā' after the alif to indicate possession, and thus Abū Jaʿfar recited it: "Yā ḥasratāy." And ḥasrah means regret.

﴿Over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: In obedience to God. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That is, in the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He said: That is, the Qur'an and acting upon it. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "In God's side" means in God's reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: The janb (side) is nearness and proximity. It is said: "So-and-so lives in the side of so-and-so," meaning in his neighborhood, and from it is "and the companion at the side" (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb), meaning: over what I neglected in seeking His neighborhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, over the path which is God's path, to which He called me. The Arabs call the cause and the path to a thing a janb. They say: "I swallowed sorrows in your side," meaning for your sake, because of you, and for the sake of your pleasure. It was also said: "In God's side" means in the direction that leads to God's pleasure and reward. The Arabs call a direction janb. The poet said:

"The heart was divided, striving for that: the people are a side, and the commander is a side."

Meaning the people from one side and the commander from another side. Ibn ʿArafah said: That is, I abandoned God's command. It is said: "I did not do that in the side of my need," meaning... Kuthayyir said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a lover, who has a heart burning for you, torn to pieces?"

Mujāhid also said likewise, meaning: I wasted some of God's command. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man sits in a sitting, nor walks a walk, nor lies down in a place, in which he does not remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it will be a tirah (a loss/burden) upon him on the Day of Resurrection," that is, a ḥasrah [Ibn al-Athīr explained it in al-Nihāyah as deficiency or liability]. Abū Dāwūd related it in meaning.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: Among the regrets of the Day of Resurrection is that a man sees his wealth, which God gave him in this world, on the Day of Resurrection in the scale of another, who inherited it and acted with it in truth, so he has its reward and the other has its burden. Among the regrets is that a man sees his slave, whom God placed under his authority in this world, nearer in rank to God, the Mighty and Majestic, or sees a man whom he knew blind in this world, now seeing on the Day of Resurrection while he himself is blind.

﴿And indeed I was among the scoffers﴾, i.e., I was only among those who mocked the Qur'an and the Messenger in this world, and the friends of God. Qatādah said: It was not enough for him that he neglected obedience to God, until he mocked its people. The place of "in kuntu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he said: "I neglected while I was mocking," i.e., I neglected in the state of my mockery. It was also said: I was only in mockery, play, and falsehood, i.e., my striving was only in the worship of other than God, the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿"If only God had guided me"﴾, i.e., had shown me the way to His religion, ﴿"I would have been among the righteous"﴾, i.e., among those who avoid polytheism and sins. This saying, "If only God had guided me, I would have been guided," is a true statement, though it is close to the argument of the polytheists about which the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, informed concerning them in His saying: "Those who associated will say: 'If God had willed, we would not have associated.'" So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

Then he put it in the accusative (naṣb). (تُسْئَلُ) is in the accusative because it agrees in position with الذكرى (remembrance), since the meaning of the sentence is: "What is it to you from it but that you remember," as in the saying: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," meaning: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," i.e., "Would that I wore a cloak and was cool."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do acts of disobedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of a man of the people of Paradise, so he enters Paradise." He said, "Why should I tire myself?" So he abandoned his deeds and took to wickedness and disobedience. Iblis said to him, "You have a long life, so enjoy the world, then repent." So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." It is as if this speaker had said, "I was not guided," so it was said, "Yes indeed, the path of guidance was made clear to you, and you were in a position where, had you wished to believe, you would have been able to believe."

"My signs" means the Qur'an. It is also said that by "the signs" are meant the miracles, i.e., the proof was clear, but you denied it and rejected it, (and you were arrogant), meaning you were too proud to believe, (and were among the disbelievers).

He said "you were arrogant and you were" in the masculine address, because the word nafs (soul/self) applies to both male and female. It is said: "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Al-Mubarrad said: The Arabs say "nafs wāḥid," meaning one person.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited: "Indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers."

Al-A'mash recited: "Bala, qad jā'athu āyātī" (in the third person), and this indicates the sense of remembrance. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas did not meet Umm Salamah, but the recitation (qirā'ah) is permissible, because nafs can apply to both masculine and feminine. Some have rejected this recitation and said: If the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra, then one must say: "wa kunti min al-kawāfir" or "min al-kāfirāt." Al-Nahhas said: This does not necessarily follow. Do you not see that before it there is: "lest a soul should say," then he said: "wa in kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn," and he did not say "min al-sawākhir" or "min al-sākhirāt." The rule in Arabic is that the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra in "wa istakbarta wa kunta" (you were arrogant and you were), which is from the plural "al-sākhirīn," or "min al-nās al-sākhirīn," or "min al-qawm al-sākhirīn."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 53–59 (part 1 of 2):

It is permissible to delete the yā' (the final ya of "ʿibādī"), because the vocative is a place of deletion. Al-Naḥḥās (a grammarian and exegete) said: Among the most excellent reports concerning it is that of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUmar, who said: When we gathered for the emigration (hijrah), I, Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī, and ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah ibn ʿUtbah agreed upon a meeting place, the ʾAḍāh (a pond) of the Banū Ghifār. We said: Whoever is delayed among us has been detained, so let his companion proceed. I and ʿAyyāsh ibn ʿUtbah arrived in the morning, but Hishām was detained from us, and then he was tested and succumbed to the test. We used to say in Medina: These people knew God, the Mighty and Majestic, and believed in His Messenger (ﷺ), then they fell into trial because of a calamity that befell them; we do not see any repentance for them. They, too, were saying this to themselves. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed in His Book: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God," up to His saying, may He be exalted: "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" ʿUmar said: So I wrote it with my own hand and sent it to Hishām. Hishām said: When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhū Ṭuwā and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us, so I returned, sat upon my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

And from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A group of the polytheists had killed much and committed fornication much, and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), or sent to him: "What you call to is good, but do you inform us that there is repentance for us?" So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves." Al-Bukhārī related it in meaning.

It has already passed at the end of al-Furqān (vol. 13, p. 76 ff., first or second edition).

And from Ibn ʿAbbās also: It was revealed concerning the people of Mecca, who said: "Muḥammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul which God has forbidden will not be forgiven. How can we emigrate and submit, when we have worshipped another god along with God and killed the soul which God has forbidden?" So God revealed this verse.

It is said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had transgressed against themselves in worship and feared that it would not be accepted from them because of sins they had committed in the pre-Islamic period (al-jāhiliyyah).

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and ʿAṭāʾ (said): It was revealed concerning Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamzah, because he thought that God would not accept his Islam. Ibn Jurayj related from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Waḥshī came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muḥammad, I have come to you seeking protection, so grant me protection until I hear the speech of God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I had wished to see you without a pact of protection. But since you have come to me seeking protection, you are under my protection until you hear the speech of God." He said: "Indeed I have associated others with God, I have killed the soul which God has forbidden, and I have committed fornication. Will God accept repentance from me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent until there was revealed: "And those who do not invoke with God another god, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, nor commit fornication" [al-Furqān: 68], up to the end of the verse. He recited it to him. He said: "I see a condition. Perhaps I will not do righteous deeds. I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 48]. He summoned him and recited it to him. He said: "Perhaps I am among those whom He does not will (to forgive). I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." He said: "Yes, now I see no condition," and he embraced Islam.

Ḥammād ibn Salamah related from Thābit, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Asmāʾ that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
