"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

Then he put it in the accusative (naṣb). (تُسْئَلُ) is in the accusative because it agrees in position with الذكرى (remembrance), since the meaning of the sentence is: "What is it to you from it but that you remember," as in the saying: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," meaning: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," i.e., "Would that I wore a cloak and was cool."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do acts of disobedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of a man of the people of Paradise, so he enters Paradise." He said, "Why should I tire myself?" So he abandoned his deeds and took to wickedness and disobedience. Iblis said to him, "You have a long life, so enjoy the world, then repent." So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." It is as if this speaker had said, "I was not guided," so it was said, "Yes indeed, the path of guidance was made clear to you, and you were in a position where, had you wished to believe, you would have been able to believe."

"My signs" means the Qur'an. It is also said that by "the signs" are meant the miracles, i.e., the proof was clear, but you denied it and rejected it, (and you were arrogant), meaning you were too proud to believe, (and were among the disbelievers).

He said "you were arrogant and you were" in the masculine address, because the word nafs (soul/self) applies to both male and female. It is said: "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Al-Mubarrad said: The Arabs say "nafs wāḥid," meaning one person.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited: "Indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers."

Al-A'mash recited: "Bala, qad jā'athu āyātī" (in the third person), and this indicates the sense of remembrance. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas did not meet Umm Salamah, but the recitation (qirā'ah) is permissible, because nafs can apply to both masculine and feminine. Some have rejected this recitation and said: If the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra, then one must say: "wa kunti min al-kawāfir" or "min al-kāfirāt." Al-Nahhas said: This does not necessarily follow. Do you not see that before it there is: "lest a soul should say," then he said: "wa in kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn," and he did not say "min al-sawākhir" or "min al-sākhirāt." The rule in Arabic is that the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra in "wa istakbarta wa kunta" (you were arrogant and you were), which is from the plural "al-sākhirīn," or "min al-nās al-sākhirīn," or "min al-qawm al-sākhirīn."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 53–59 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾. It is permissible to delete the yā' (the final ya of "ʿibādī"), because the vocative is a place of deletion. Al-Naḥḥās (a grammarian and exegete) said: Among the most excellent reports concerning it is that of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUmar, who said: When we gathered for the emigration (hijrah), I, Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī, and ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah ibn ʿUtbah agreed upon a meeting place, the ʾAḍāh (a pond) of the Banū Ghifār. We said: Whoever is delayed among us has been detained, so let his companion proceed. I and ʿAyyāsh ibn ʿUtbah arrived in the morning, but Hishām was detained from us, and then he was tested and succumbed to the test. We used to say in Medina: These people knew God, the Mighty and Majestic, and believed in His Messenger (ﷺ), then they fell into trial because of a calamity that befell them; we do not see any repentance for them. They, too, were saying this to themselves. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed in His Book: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God," up to His saying, may He be exalted: "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" ʿUmar said: So I wrote it with my own hand and sent it to Hishām. Hishām said: When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhū Ṭuwā and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us, so I returned, sat upon my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

And from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A group of the polytheists had killed much and committed fornication much, and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), or sent to him: "What you call to is good, but do you inform us that there is repentance for us?" So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves." Al-Bukhārī related it in meaning.

It has already passed at the end of al-Furqān (vol. 13, p. 76 ff., first or second edition).

And from Ibn ʿAbbās also: It was revealed concerning the people of Mecca, who said: "Muḥammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul which God has forbidden will not be forgiven. How can we emigrate and submit, when we have worshipped another god along with God and killed the soul which God has forbidden?" So God revealed this verse.

It is said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had transgressed against themselves in worship and feared that it would not be accepted from them because of sins they had committed in the pre-Islamic period (al-jāhiliyyah).

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and ʿAṭāʾ (said): It was revealed concerning Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamzah, because he thought that God would not accept his Islam. Ibn Jurayj related from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Waḥshī came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muḥammad, I have come to you seeking protection, so grant me protection until I hear the speech of God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I had wished to see you without a pact of protection. But since you have come to me seeking protection, you are under my protection until you hear the speech of God." He said: "Indeed I have associated others with God, I have killed the soul which God has forbidden, and I have committed fornication. Will God accept repentance from me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent until there was revealed: "And those who do not invoke with God another god, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, nor commit fornication" [al-Furqān: 68], up to the end of the verse. He recited it to him. He said: "I see a condition. Perhaps I will not do righteous deeds. I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 48]. He summoned him and recited it to him. He said: "Perhaps I am among those whom He does not will (to forgive). I am under your protection until I hear the speech of God." Then there was revealed: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." He said: "Yes, now I see no condition," and he embraced Islam.

Ḥammād ibn Salamah related from Thābit, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Asmāʾ that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd: "Indeed God forgives all sins, for whomever He wills."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: These two readings are by way of explanation, i.e., God forgives whomever He wills. God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows whom He wills to forgive, namely the penitent, or one who committed a minor sin and had no major sin. This indicates that He intends the penitent by what follows: "And turn in repentance to your Lord." So the penitent has all his sins forgiven. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 82]. This is without difficulty.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: There is no verse in the Qur'an broader in scope than this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." This has already passed in (sūrat) Subḥān (vol. 1, p. 322 ff., first or second edition).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās refuted them and said: The most hopeful verse in the Qur'an is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. This has passed in (sūrat) al-Raʿd (vol. 9, p. 285, first or second edition).

It is read "wa-lā taqnaṭū" with kasrah and with fatḥah on the nūn. Its explanation has passed in (sūrat) al-Ḥijr (vol. 10, p. 36, first or second edition).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾, i.e., return to Him in obedience. When He explained that whoever repents from polytheism will be forgiven, He commanded repentance and return to Him. Inābah (turning in repentance) is returning to God with sincerity.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, i.e., humble yourselves before Him and obey Him, ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ in this world, ﴿then you will not be helped﴾, i.e., you will not be prevented from His punishment. It is related in a ḥadīth from Jābir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among happiness is that God lengthens a person's life in obedience and grants him inābah, and indeed among wretchedness is that a person does deeds and is pleased with his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. "The best of what was sent down" is the Qur'an, and all of it is good. The meaning, as al-Ḥasan said: Adhere to His obedience and avoid His disobedience. Al-Suddī said: The best is what God commanded in His Book. Ibn Zayd said: That is, the clear (muḥkam) verses, and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābih) to its knower. He said: God sent down books, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms, then He sent down the Qur'an and commanded following it, so it is the best and it is the inimitable (muʿjiz). It was also said: This is the best because it abrogates and supersedes all the books, while all the books are abrogated. It was said: It means pardon, because God gave His Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice between pardon and retaliation. It was said: What God taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) that is not Qur'an is good, and what was revealed to him of the Qur'an is the best. It was said: The best of what was sent down to you is the reports of the past nations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me"﴾. The "an" (lest) is in the accusative position, meaning "out of dislike that a soul should say." According to the Kufans it means "so that it does not say," and according to the Basrans it means "for fear that it says." It was said: That is, "lest a soul say," because He said before this: "before the punishment comes upon you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why is "nafs" indefinite? I say: Because what is meant by it is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that it means a soul distinguished from the (other) souls, either by intense obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that it means multiplicity, as al-Aʿshā said:

"And many a open space, if I shouted in its air, a noble man would come to me shaking his head in anger."

He means groups of nobles who would help him, not a single noble, and its parallel is: "Many a land have I crossed, and many a champion have I fought," where only multiplicity is intended.

"Yā ḥasratā": the original is "yā ḥasratī," and the yā' was replaced by an alif, because it is lighter and more suited to prolonging the voice in calling out (istighāthah). They sometimes attach a hā' to it. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O welcome, O donkey that is swift..." (al-Nājiyah: swift; in al-Farrāʾ's tafsīr it is "nāhiyah" instead of "nājiyah," and so it is related in al-Lisān and Sharḥ al-Qāmūs under the root sanā. Here al-sāniyah is a verbal noun on the pattern fāʿilah meaning irrigation; he meant his water-skin for irrigating.)
"When he comes, I bring him near to the irrigating (camel)."

They sometimes attach a yā' after the alif to indicate possession, and thus Abū Jaʿfar recited it: "Yā ḥasratāy." And ḥasrah means regret.

﴿Over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: In obedience to God. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That is, in the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He said: That is, the Qur'an and acting upon it. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "In God's side" means in God's reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: The janb (side) is nearness and proximity. It is said: "So-and-so lives in the side of so-and-so," meaning in his neighborhood, and from it is "and the companion at the side" (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb), meaning: over what I neglected in seeking His neighborhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, over the path which is God's path, to which He called me. The Arabs call the cause and the path to a thing a janb. They say: "I swallowed sorrows in your side," meaning for your sake, because of you, and for the sake of your pleasure. It was also said: "In God's side" means in the direction that leads to God's pleasure and reward. The Arabs call a direction janb. The poet said:

"The heart was divided, striving for that: the people are a side, and the commander is a side."

Meaning the people from one side and the commander from another side. Ibn ʿArafah said: That is, I abandoned God's command. It is said: "I did not do that in the side of my need," meaning... Kuthayyir said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a lover, who has a heart burning for you, torn to pieces?"

Mujāhid also said likewise, meaning: I wasted some of God's command. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man sits in a sitting, nor walks a walk, nor lies down in a place, in which he does not remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it will be a tirah (a loss/burden) upon him on the Day of Resurrection," that is, a ḥasrah [Ibn al-Athīr explained it in al-Nihāyah as deficiency or liability]. Abū Dāwūd related it in meaning.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: Among the regrets of the Day of Resurrection is that a man sees his wealth, which God gave him in this world, on the Day of Resurrection in the scale of another, who inherited it and acted with it in truth, so he has its reward and the other has its burden. Among the regrets is that a man sees his slave, whom God placed under his authority in this world, nearer in rank to God, the Mighty and Majestic, or sees a man whom he knew blind in this world, now seeing on the Day of Resurrection while he himself is blind.

﴿And indeed I was among the scoffers﴾, i.e., I was only among those who mocked the Qur'an and the Messenger in this world, and the friends of God. Qatādah said: It was not enough for him that he neglected obedience to God, until he mocked its people. The place of "in kuntu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he said: "I neglected while I was mocking," i.e., I neglected in the state of my mockery. It was also said: I was only in mockery, play, and falsehood, i.e., my striving was only in the worship of other than God, the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿"If only God had guided me"﴾, i.e., had shown me the way to His religion, ﴿"I would have been among the righteous"﴾, i.e., among those who avoid polytheism and sins. This saying, "If only God had guided me, I would have been guided," is a true statement, though it is close to the argument of the polytheists about which the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, informed concerning them in His saying: "Those who associated will say: 'If God had willed, we would not have associated.'" So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." Indeed God forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd: "Indeed God forgives all sins, for whomever He wills."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: These two readings are by way of explanation, i.e., God forgives whomever He wills. God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows whom He wills to forgive, namely the penitent, or one who committed a minor sin and had no major sin. This indicates that He intends the penitent by what follows: "And turn in repentance to your Lord." So the penitent has all his sins forgiven. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 82]. This is without difficulty.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: There is no verse in the Qur'an broader in scope than this verse: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God." This has already passed in (sūrat) Subḥān (vol. 1, p. 322 ff., first or second edition).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās refuted them and said: The most hopeful verse in the Qur'an is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. This has passed in (sūrat) al-Raʿd (vol. 9, p. 285, first or second edition).

It is read "wa-lā taqnaṭū" with kasrah and with fatḥah on the nūn. Its explanation has passed in (sūrat) al-Ḥijr (vol. 10, p. 36, first or second edition).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾, i.e., return to Him in obedience. When He explained that whoever repents from polytheism will be forgiven, He commanded repentance and return to Him. Inābah (turning in repentance) is returning to God with sincerity.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, i.e., humble yourselves before Him and obey Him, ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ in this world, ﴿then you will not be helped﴾, i.e., you will not be prevented from His punishment. It is related in a ḥadīth from Jābir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among happiness is that God lengthens a person's life in obedience and grants him inābah, and indeed among wretchedness is that a person does deeds and is pleased with his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. "The best of what was sent down" is the Qur'an, and all of it is good. The meaning, as al-Ḥasan said: Adhere to His obedience and avoid His disobedience. Al-Suddī said: The best is what God commanded in His Book. Ibn Zayd said: That is, the clear (muḥkam) verses, and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous (mutashābih) to its knower. He said: God sent down books, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms, then He sent down the Qur'an and commanded following it, so it is the best and it is the inimitable (muʿjiz). It was also said: This is the best because it abrogates and supersedes all the books, while all the books are abrogated. It was said: It means pardon, because God gave His Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice between pardon and retaliation. It was said: What God taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) that is not Qur'an is good, and what was revealed to him of the Qur'an is the best. It was said: The best of what was sent down to you is the reports of the past nations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me"﴾. The "an" (lest) is in the accusative position, meaning "out of dislike that a soul should say." According to the Kufans it means "so that it does not say," and according to the Basrans it means "for fear that it says." It was said: That is, "lest a soul say," because He said before this: "before the punishment comes upon you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why is "nafs" indefinite? I say: Because what is meant by it is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that it means a soul distinguished from the (other) souls, either by intense obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that it means multiplicity, as al-Aʿshā said:

"And many a open space, if I shouted in its air, a noble man would come to me shaking his head in anger."

He means groups of nobles who would help him, not a single noble, and its parallel is: "Many a land have I crossed, and many a champion have I fought," where only multiplicity is intended.

"Yā ḥasratā": the original is "yā ḥasratī," and the yā' was replaced by an alif, because it is lighter and more suited to prolonging the voice in calling out (istighāthah). They sometimes attach a hā' to it. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O welcome, O donkey that is swift..." (al-Nājiyah: swift; in al-Farrāʾ's tafsīr it is "nāhiyah" instead of "nājiyah," and so it is related in al-Lisān and Sharḥ al-Qāmūs under the root sanā. Here al-sāniyah is a verbal noun on the pattern fāʿilah meaning irrigation; he meant his water-skin for irrigating.)
"When he comes, I bring him near to the irrigating (camel)."

They sometimes attach a yā' after the alif to indicate possession, and thus Abū Jaʿfar recited it: "Yā ḥasratāy." And ḥasrah means regret.

﴿Over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: In obedience to God. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That is, in the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He said: That is, the Qur'an and acting upon it. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "In God's side" means in God's reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: The janb (side) is nearness and proximity. It is said: "So-and-so lives in the side of so-and-so," meaning in his neighborhood, and from it is "and the companion at the side" (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb), meaning: over what I neglected in seeking His neighborhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, over the path which is God's path, to which He called me. The Arabs call the cause and the path to a thing a janb. They say: "I swallowed sorrows in your side," meaning for your sake, because of you, and for the sake of your pleasure. It was also said: "In God's side" means in the direction that leads to God's pleasure and reward. The Arabs call a direction janb. The poet said:

"The heart was divided, striving for that: the people are a side, and the commander is a side."

Meaning the people from one side and the commander from another side. Ibn ʿArafah said: That is, I abandoned God's command. It is said: "I did not do that in the side of my need," meaning... Kuthayyir said:

"Will you not fear God regarding a lover, who has a heart burning for you, torn to pieces?"

Mujāhid also said likewise, meaning: I wasted some of God's command. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man sits in a sitting, nor walks a walk, nor lies down in a place, in which he does not remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it will be a tirah (a loss/burden) upon him on the Day of Resurrection," that is, a ḥasrah [Ibn al-Athīr explained it in al-Nihāyah as deficiency or liability]. Abū Dāwūd related it in meaning.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: Among the regrets of the Day of Resurrection is that a man sees his wealth, which God gave him in this world, on the Day of Resurrection in the scale of another, who inherited it and acted with it in truth, so he has its reward and the other has its burden. Among the regrets is that a man sees his slave, whom God placed under his authority in this world, nearer in rank to God, the Mighty and Majestic, or sees a man whom he knew blind in this world, now seeing on the Day of Resurrection while he himself is blind.

﴿And indeed I was among the scoffers﴾, i.e., I was only among those who mocked the Qur'an and the Messenger in this world, and the friends of God. Qatādah said: It was not enough for him that he neglected obedience to God, until he mocked its people. The place of "in kuntu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he said: "I neglected while I was mocking," i.e., I neglected in the state of my mockery. It was also said: I was only in mockery, play, and falsehood, i.e., my striving was only in the worship of other than God, the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿"If only God had guided me"﴾, i.e., had shown me the way to His religion, ﴿"I would have been among the righteous"﴾, i.e., among those who avoid polytheism and sins. This saying, "If only God had guided me, I would have been guided," is a true statement, though it is close to the argument of the polytheists about which the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, informed concerning them in His saying: "Those who associated will say: 'If God had willed, we would not have associated.'" So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

Then he put it in the accusative (naṣb). (تُسْئَلُ) is in the accusative because it agrees in position with الذكرى (remembrance), since the meaning of the sentence is: "What is it to you from it but that you remember," as in the saying: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," meaning: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," i.e., "Would that I wore a cloak and was cool."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do acts of disobedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of a man of the people of Paradise, so he enters Paradise." He said, "Why should I tire myself?" So he abandoned his deeds and took to wickedness and disobedience. Iblis said to him, "You have a long life, so enjoy the world, then repent." So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." It is as if this speaker had said, "I was not guided," so it was said, "Yes indeed, the path of guidance was made clear to you, and you were in a position where, had you wished to believe, you would have been able to believe."

"My signs" means the Qur'an. It is also said that by "the signs" are meant the miracles, i.e., the proof was clear, but you denied it and rejected it, (and you were arrogant), meaning you were too proud to believe, (and were among the disbelievers).

He said "you were arrogant and you were" in the masculine address, because the word nafs (soul/self) applies to both male and female. It is said: "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Al-Mubarrad said: The Arabs say "nafs wāḥid," meaning one person.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited: "Indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers."

Al-A'mash recited: "Bala, qad jā'athu āyātī" (in the third person), and this indicates the sense of remembrance. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas did not meet Umm Salamah, but the recitation (qirā'ah) is permissible, because nafs can apply to both masculine and feminine. Some have rejected this recitation and said: If the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra, then one must say: "wa kunti min al-kawāfir" or "min al-kāfirāt." Al-Nahhas said: This does not necessarily follow. Do you not see that before it there is: "lest a soul should say," then he said: "wa in kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn," and he did not say "min al-sawākhir" or "min al-sākhirāt." The rule in Arabic is that the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra in "wa istakbarta wa kunta" (you were arrogant and you were), which is from the plural "al-sākhirīn," or "min al-nās al-sākhirīn," or "min al-qawm al-sākhirīn."

We said: Whoever is delayed among us has been detained, so let his companion proceed. I and ʿAyyāsh ibn ʿUtbah arrived in the morning, but Hishām was detained from us, and then he was tested and succumbed to the test. We used to say in Medina: These people knew God, the Mighty and Majestic, and believed in His Messenger (ﷺ), then they fell into trial because of a calamity that befell them; we do not see any repentance for them. They, too, were saying this to themselves. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed in His Book: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God," up to His saying, may He be exalted: "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" ʿUmar said: So I wrote it with my own hand and sent it to Hishām. Hishām said: When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhū Ṭuwā and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us, so I returned, sat upon my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

It has already passed at the end of al-Furqān (vol. 13, p. 76 ff., first or second edition).

It is said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had transgressed against themselves in worship and feared that it would not be accepted from them because of sins they had committed in the pre-Islamic period (al-jāhiliyyah).

So it is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, just as ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said when one of the Khawārij said: "There is no judgment except for God."

﴿Or says﴾ — this soul — ﴿when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return"﴾, i.e., a return to the world, ﴿so that I would be among the doers of good﴾. The verb "fa-akūna" is in the accusative as a response to the wish (tamannī). If you wish, it may be coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "kar­atan," because its meaning is "that I return," as the poet said:

"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye are dearer to me than wearing sheer garments."

Al-Farrāʾ also recited:

فَمَا لَكَ مِنْهَا غَيْرُ ذِكْرَى وَخَشْيَةٍ ... وَتَسْأَلَ عَنْ رُكْبَانِهَا أَيْنَ يَمَّمُوا فنصب

Then he put it in the accusative (naṣb). (تُسْئَلُ) is in the accusative because it agrees in position with الذكرى (remembrance), since the meaning of the sentence is: "What is it to you from it but that you remember," as in the saying: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," meaning: "It is not for me to wear a cloak and be cool," i.e., "Would that I wore a cloak and was cool."

Abu Salih said: There was a learned man among the Children of Israel who found a scrap of writing: "Indeed, a servant may do the works of obedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of the people of the Fire, so he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do acts of disobedience to Allah for a long time, and then his deed is concluded with the deed of a man of the people of Paradise, so he enters Paradise." He said, "Why should I tire myself?" So he abandoned his deeds and took to wickedness and disobedience. Iblis said to him, "You have a long life, so enjoy the world, then repent." So he persisted in wickedness and spent his wealth in immorality. Then the Angel of Death came to him while he was at his most pleasurable state. He said, "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! My life has passed in the obedience of Satan." He regretted when regret no longer benefited him. So Allah revealed his account in the Qur'an.

Qatadah said: These are categories. One group of them said: "Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah." Another group of them said: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing." Another said: "Had I a return, I would be among the good-doers." Then Allah, Exalted, responded to their words: (Yes, indeed, My signs came to you).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" (yes indeed) is the answer to a negation, and there is no negative word in the sentence. But the meaning of "Had Allah guided me" is "He did not guide me." It is as if this speaker had said, "I was not guided," so it was said, "Yes indeed, the path of guidance was made clear to you, and you were in a position where, had you wished to believe, you would have been able to believe."

"My signs" means the Qur'an. It is also said that by "the signs" are meant the miracles, i.e., the proof was clear, but you denied it and rejected it, (and you were arrogant), meaning you were too proud to believe, (and were among the disbelievers).

He said "you were arrogant and you were" in the masculine address, because the word nafs (soul/self) applies to both male and female. It is said: "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Al-Mubarrad said: The Arabs say "nafs wāḥid," meaning one person.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited: "Indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers."

Al-A'mash recited: "Bala, qad jā'athu āyātī" (in the third person), and this indicates the sense of remembrance. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas did not meet Umm Salamah, but the recitation (qirā'ah) is permissible, because nafs can apply to both masculine and feminine. Some have rejected this recitation and said: If the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra, then one must say: "wa kunti min al-kawāfir" or "min al-kāfirāt." Al-Nahhas said: This does not necessarily follow. Do you not see that before it there is: "lest a soul should say," then he said: "wa in kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn," and he did not say "min al-sawākhir" or "min al-sākhirāt." The rule in Arabic is that the taʾ is pronounced with a kasra in "wa istakbarta wa kunta" (you were arrogant and you were), which is from the plural "al-sākhirīn," or "min al-nās al-sākhirīn," or "min al-qawm al-sākhirīn."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 60–64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah, their faces blackened﴾. That is, by what encompassed them of Allah's anger and vengeance. Al-Akhfash said: "tara" (you see) does not govern "wujuhuhum musawwadah" (their faces are blackened); rather it is an inceptive subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) if "tara" is from sight (ru'yat al-basar), and a second object if it is from the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb). ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the meaning of arrogance (kibr), and he (peace be upon him) said: "Rejecting the truth and looking down on people" (ghamt al-nas), that is, despising them. This has passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 296, second or third edition.]] and elsewhere. And in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like specks (al-dharr), disgrace overtaking them from every side, until they are brought to the prison of Hell (sijn Jahannam)."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him﴾. It is also read "wayunjī" (yunjī), that is, from shirk and sins.

(bi-mafazatihim) with the singular form is the reading of the general readers, since it is a verbal noun (masdar). The Kufans read "bi-mafazatihim" (plural), and this is permissible, just as you say "bi-sa'adatihim." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), explaining this verse, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Allah will gather with each person his deed, so the deed of the believer will be with him in the most beautiful form and the sweetest fragrance. Whenever there is terror or fear, he will say to him: 'Do not be alarmed, for you are not the one it is aimed at, nor are you the one it concerns.' When that becomes heavy upon him, he will say: 'How beautiful you are! Who are you?' He will reply: 'Do you not recognize me? I am your righteous deed, which carried you in your weight. By Allah, I will carry you and defend you.' This is what Allah meant: ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him with their achievement; evil will not touch them, nor will they grieve﴾."

(Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is Guardian over all things) i.e., Preserver and Sustainer of them, and this has already been mentioned.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth﴾. Its singular is miqlid. It is also said: miqlad, and most often used is iqlid. Al-Maqalid means the keys, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Al-Suddi said: the treasuries of the heavens and the earth. Others said: the treasuries of the heavens are the rain, and the treasuries of the earth are the plants. There is another dialect, aqalid, and in that case its singular is iqlid. Al-Jawhari said: al-iqlid is the key, and al-miqlad is a key like a sickle (minjal), with which grass is cut, just as the hay (qatt) is cut when made into ropes, i.e., it is cut. The plural is al-maqalid. And "aqlada al-bahr 'ala khalq katheer" means it drowned them, as if it locked them in. Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Umar that Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one has asked me about it: There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, I seek Allah's forgiveness, and there is no power nor might except with Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. He gives life and causes death, in His hand is the good, and He is over all things Powerful." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it in his tafsir, and he added: whoever says it when he rises in the morning or the evening ten times, Allah will grant him six qualities: the first, he will be guarded from Iblis; the second, twelve thousand angels will attend him; the third, he will be given a qintar (a great measure) of reward; the fourth, a degree will be raised for him; the fifth, Allah will marry him to the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in); and the sixth, he will have a reward like one who recited the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, and he will also have a reward like one who performed Hajj and 'Umrah, and his Hajj and 'Umrah will be accepted. If he dies that night, he dies as a martyr. Al-Harith narrated from Ali who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the interpretation of the maqalid, and he said: "O Ali, you have asked about something great. The maqalid is that you say ten times when you rise in the morning and ten times when you enter the evening: There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, glory be to Allah, all praise is to Allah, I seek Allah's forgiveness, and there is no power except with Allah, the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs the praise, in His hand is the good, and He is over all things Powerful." Whoever says it ten times in the morning and ten times in the evening, Allah will grant him six qualities: the first, He will guard him from Satan and his soldiers, so they will have no authority over him; the second, he will be given a qintar in Paradise, which is heavier in his scale than Mount Uhud; the third, a degree will be raised for him that none attain except the righteous; the fourth, Allah will marry him to the wide-eyed houris; the fifth, twelve thousand angels will witness it for him, writing it for him on an unrolled scroll and bearing witness for him on the Day of Resurrection; and the sixth, he will have a reward as if he had recited the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Criterion (al-Furqan), and as one who performed Hajj and 'Umrah, and Allah will accept his Hajj and 'Umrah. If he dies that day, or that night, or that month, he is sealed with the seal of the martyrs. It is also said: al-maqalid means obedience. It is said: "alqa ila fulan bi'l-maqalid," meaning he obeyed him in what he commanded. So the meaning of the verse is: to Him belongs the obedience of whoever is in the heavens and the earth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, in the Qur'an, the proofs and the indications.

(Those are the losers) has already been discussed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you then command me to worship other than Allah?﴾ (This was when they invited the Prophet (ﷺ) to what they were upon of worshipping idols, and they said: "It is the religion of your fathers.") "Ghayr" is in the accusative governed by "a'bud" according to the estimate: "a'bud ghayr Allah fima ta'murunani" (I worship other than Allah in what you command me). It is also permissible for it to be governed by "ta'murunni" by omitting the preposition; the estimate: "Do you command me with other than Allah, that I worship?" since "an" is implied and "an" with the verb forms a verbal noun, and it is in apposition to "ghayr." The estimate: "Do you command me with the worship of other than Allah?" Nafi' read "ta'murunni" with one light nun and an open ya'. Ibn 'Amir read "ta'murunani" with two light nuns, according to the original form. The rest read with one heavy (shaddah) nun, by assimilation (idgham), and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because it occurs in the Mushaf of Uthman with one nun. Nafi' read with the second nun omitted; it was the second that was omitted because the repetition and the heaviness fall upon it. Also, omitting the first is not permissible, because it is the indicator of the nominative case. Its explanation has passed in al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 29, first or second edition.]] at His saying: "Atuhajjunni." "A'bud," i.e., "an a'bud" (that I worship); when "an" was omitted, it took the nominative, as al-Kisa'i said, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Ala ayyuha al-zajiri ahdur al-wagha
(Unquestioning, O you who forbid me to attend the battle,)
[[The line is from the Mu'allaqa of Tarafah, and its completion is: "wa-an ashhada al-ladhdhat hal anta mukhalladi" (and that I witness pleasures; will you make me immortal?).]]

The evidence for the soundness of this view is the reading of the one who read "a'bud" in the accusative.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verses 65–66:**

God's words: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be nullified."﴾ It was said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended meaning is: "It has certainly been revealed to you: 'If you associate others with God...,' and it was revealed to those before you likewise." It was also said: it is on its own (literal) basis. Muqatil said: meaning, it was revealed to you and to the prophets before you concerning tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and the word tawhid is omitted. Then He said: "If you associate others with God, O Muhammad (ﷺ), your deeds will surely be nullified." This is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically. It was also said: the address is to him, but what is meant is his community, since God knows that he will not associate others with God and that no association will occur from him. "Ihbat" (nullification) means invalidation and corruption. Al-Qushayri said: whoever apostatizes, his previous acts of obedience do not benefit him. However, the nullification of deeds by apostasy is conditional upon dying in disbelief, and for this reason He said: ﴿Whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void﴾. Thus the absolute (mutlaq) is interpreted in light of the qualified (muqayyad). For this reason we say: whoever performs the hajj, then apostatizes, then returns to Islam, is not obligated to repeat the hajj. I say: this is the position of al-Shafi'i, while according to Malik he is obligated to repeat it. The full explanation of this has already passed in surat al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 3, p. 48, first or second edition.]]

God's words: ﴿Rather, worship God alone﴾. Al-Nahhas said: in my book, from Abu Ishaq, the word ism Allah ("the name of God") is in the accusative, governed by the verb "a'budu" (I worship). He said: there is no disagreement about this between the Basrans and the Kufans. Al-Nahhas said: al-Farra' said it is in the accusative by a suppressed verb. Al-Mahdawi related this from al-Kisa'i. As for the fa' in "fa-a'bud", al-Zajjaj said it is for conditional response (al-mujazah), and al-Akhfash said it is extra (za'idah). Ibn Abbas said: "fa-a'bud" means "fa-wahhid" (so affirm the oneness). Others said: "bal Allah" means "fa-ati' Allah" (so obey God). ﴿And be among the grateful﴾ for His blessings, unlike the polytheists.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 39, verses 67–68:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have not measured God with His true measure﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "They did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, from your saying, 'So-and-so is of great worth (ʿazim al-qadr).'" Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning according to this is: 'They did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, when they worshipped others along with Him, while He is the Creator of things and their Owner.' Then He informed about His power and greatness, saying: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾." Then He declared Himself free of being like a limb, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾.

In al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), who said: A Jewish man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, God holds the heavens on one finger and the creatures on one finger, then He says: 'I am the King.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molar teeth showed, then said: "﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾." He (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan (good) ṣaḥīḥ (sound)."

In al-Bukhari and Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God will seize the earth on the Day of Resurrection and fold the heaven in His right hand, then He will say: 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?'"

In al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of ʿĀʾisha, that she asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His saying: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. She said: "I said: 'Then where will people be on that day, O Messenger of God?'" He said: "On the bridge of Hell." In another narration: "On the Ṣirāṭ (bridge), O ʿĀʾisha." He said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."

His saying: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful﴾ and "God will seize the earth" is an expression for His power and His encompassing of all His creatures. It is said: "So-and-so is only in my grasp," meaning: "So-and-so is only in my power." People say: "Things are in His grasp," meaning: in His dominion and power.

The meaning of "seizing" and "folding" may also be the annihilation and removal of a thing. So His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful﴾ may mean: "The earth entirely will be gone and perishing on the Day of Resurrection." It is said: "What we were in has folded away from us, and something else has come to us," and "a time (dahr) has folded away from us," meaning: passed and gone.

"Yamin" (right hand) in the speech of the Arabs may also mean power and dominion. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: what you own. And He said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾, meaning: by strength and power, that is, We would have seized his strength and his power. Al-Farraʾ and al-Mubarrad said: "Yamin means strength and power," and they cited:

*"When a banner is raised for glory,*
*ʿArāba receives it with the right hand."*
[[The speaker is al-Ḥuṭayʾa; it is also said to be by al-Shammākh.]]

Another said:

*"When I saw the sun, its light had shone,*
*I took my need from it with the right hand."*
[[Thus it stands in the original sources, and we have not found these two verses in the references available to us.]]

*"I killed Shunayf, then Fārān after him,*
*and he was not trustworthy regarding the signs."*

[[See vol. 1, p. 142, of the second or third edition.]] For this reason He said in the hadith: "Then He will say: 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?'" We have expanded on this topic in al-Tadhkira with further explanation. We have also discussed the mention of the left hand in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, his saying: "Then He will fold the earth in His left hand."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾. This explains what happens after the seizing of the earth and the folding of the heaven, which is the blowing of the Horn (ṣūr). Ibn Majah recorded it in the Sunan. In the book of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned the companion of the Horn and said: "On his right is Jibrāʾīl and on his left is Mīkāʾīl."

They differed concerning those excepted: who are they? It has been said: they are the martyrs, wearing their swords around the Throne. This is narrated as a marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet) report from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, as al-Qushayri mentioned, and from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, as al-Thaʿlabi mentioned. It has also been said: they are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. It was also narrated from the hadith of Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾. They said: "O Prophet of God, who are those whom God excepted?" He said: "They are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl and the Angel of Death. Then God will say to the Angel of Death: 'O Angel of Death, who remains of My creation, and He knows best?' He will say: 'O Lord, Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl remain, and Your weak servant, the Angel of Death.' God, Exalted, will say: 'Take the souls of Isrāfīl and Mīkāʾīl.' So they will fall dead like two great mountains. Then He will say: 'Die, O Angel of Death,' and he will die. Then God, Exalted, will say to Jibrīl: 'O Jibrīl, who remains?' He will say: 'Blessed and exalted are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor. Your Face remains, living and everlasting, and Jibrīl is the dying, perishing one.' God, Exalted, will say: 'O Jibrīl, there is no escape from your death.' Then he will fall prostrate, beating his wings, saying: 'Glory be to You, my Lord, blessed and exalted are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The excellence of His creation over the creation of Mīkāʾīl is like a great mountain over a small hill." [[al-Ẓarb is a small mountain; its plural is ẓarāb, and in the paucal it may be pluralized as aẓrub.]] Al-Thaʿlabi mentioned it, and al-Nahhas also mentioned it from the hadith of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Yazīd al-Raqqāshī, from Anas ibn Mālik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿Then whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾. He said: "Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, the bearers of the Throne, the Angel of Death and Isrāfīl." In this hadith: "The last of them to die will be Jibrīl, peace be upon him and upon them all."

The hadith of Abu Hurayra about the martyrs is more sound, as has preceded in al-Naml. [[See vol. 13, p. 241, first or second edition.]] Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "They are Riḍwān, the ḥūr (companions of paradise), Mālik and the zabāniya (guardians of Hell)." It was also said: "They are the scorpions and serpents of the people of the Fire." Al-Ḥasan said: "They are God, the One, the Subduer, and no one from the people of the heavens and the earth remains except that He makes him taste death." Qatāda said: "God knows best what is excepted." It was also said: the exception in His saying: ﴿except whom God wills﴾ refers to those who died before the first blowing, meaning: whoever is in the heavens and the earth will die, except those whose death has already preceded, because they had already died.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and Ibn Majah, and the wording is his, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: A man of the Jews in the market of Medina said: "By Him who chose Mūsā above mankind!" A man of the Anṣār raised his hand and slapped him. He said: "Do you say this while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is among us?"

I mentioned that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾. I will be the first to raise his head, and behold, Mūsā will be holding onto one of the legs of the Throne. I do not know whether he raised his head before me, or whether he was among those whom God excepted. And whoever says 'I am better than Yūnus ibn Mattā' has lied." Al-Tirmidhi also recorded it and said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."

Al-Qushayri said: "Whoever takes the exception to refer to Mūsā and the martyrs, these have died, but they are living with God. I say: In some chains of Abu Hurayra it is reported that he (ﷺ) said: "Do not make me better than Mūsā, for people will swoon, and I will be the first to regain consciousness, and behold, Mūsā will be gripping the side of the Throne [[Gripping the side of the Throne: that is, holding on to it with strength.]]. I do not know whether he was among those who swooned and regained consciousness before me, or whether he was among those whom God excepted." Muslim recorded it, and something similar from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri. Regaining consciousness only happens after a faint and loss of reason, not after death followed by the return of life. And God knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾. That is: then behold, the dead of the people of the earth and the heavens will be living, raised from their graves, and their bodies and souls will be returned to them, and they will stand looking to see what they are commanded. It was also said: standing on their feet, looking toward the resurrection that they were promised. And it was said: this looking means waiting, that is, they wait to see what will be done to them. Al-Kisāʾī permitted *qiyāman* in the accusative, as you say: "I went out, and behold, Zayd was seated."

The meaning of "with the light of its Lord" is "with the justice of its Lord," as said by al-Hasan and others. al-Dahhak said: "with the judgment of its Lord." The meaning is one: that it shone and gave light by the justice of God and His judgment with truth among His servants. Injustice is darkness, and justice is light.

It is also said that God will create a light on the Day of Resurrection which He will cast upon the face of the earth, so the earth will shine with it. Ibn 'Abbas said: the light mentioned here is not the light of the sun and the moon, but a light which God creates, by which He illumines the earth. It is related that on that day the earth will be of silver, shining with the light of God, the Exalted, when He comes to decide the judgment. The meaning is that it shone with a light which God the Exalted created, and He attributed the light to Himself in the manner of the attribution of ownership to the owner.

It is also said that this is the day on which He will judge among His creation, for it is a day with no night in it.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read *"wa-ashraqat al-ardu"* in the passive form (*ʿalā mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu*), and this is a reading that serves as an explanation. Some people have strayed here, and imagined that God, the Mighty and Majestic, is of the same kind as perceptible light and radiance. He is exalted above the (resemblance) [[In the originals: "mubayanat al-mahsusat" (difference from perceptible things), which is a distortion.]] of perceptible things. Rather, He is the illuminator of the heavens and the earth, and from Him comes every light, in creation and origination.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "and the earth will shine with the light of its Lord," clarifies the hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) through many sound chains: "You will see your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and you will not be harmed in seeing Him." It is transmitted in four forms: *lā tuḍāmūna*, *lā tuḍārūna*, *lā tuḍāmmūna*, and *lā tuḍārrūna*. The meaning of "*lā tuḍāmūna*" is that no oppression will befall you, as it befalls you in this world when looking at kings. "*Lā tuḍārūna*" means no harm will befall you. "*Lā tuḍāmmūna*" means that none of you will press against another to ask Him to show Himself. And "*lā tuḍārrūna*" means that none of you will oppose another. It is said: *ḍārrahu muḍārrah* and *ḍirāran*, meaning he opposed him.

His saying, "And the Book will be placed": he said regarding Ibn 'Abbas: it means the Preserved Tablet. Qatadah said: it means the Book and the scrolls in which the deeds of the children of Adam are recorded, so one will take his record in his right hand and another in his left.

"And the prophets will be brought": that is, they will be brought, and He will ask them what their peoples answered them.

"And the witnesses": those who bore witness over the nations from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as the Almighty said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. It is also said that the intended witnesses are those who were martyred in the way of God, who will testify on the Day of Resurrection for those who defended the religion of God. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn Zayd said: they are the guardian angels who bear witness over people concerning their deeds. God the Exalted said: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. The driver drives it to the reckoning, and the witness bears witness against it, and this is the angel assigned to the human being, as will be explained in [Qaf, verse 21 of the said surah].

"And it will be judged between them with truth": that is, with truthfulness and justice.

"And they will not be wronged": Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: their good deeds will not be diminished, nor will their evil deeds be increased.

"And every soul will be paid in full for what it did," whether good or evil.

"And He is most knowing of what they do": in this world. And He, Mighty and Majestic, has no need of a book or of a witness; yet the books are made to testify, as a means of establishing the proof.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "and the earth will shine with the light of its Lord," clarifies the hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) through many sound chains: "You will see your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and you will not be harmed in seeing Him." The meaning of "*lā tuḍāmūna*" is that no oppression will befall you, as it befalls you in this world when looking at kings. "*Lā tuḍārūna*" means no harm will befall you. "*Lā tuḍāmmūna*" means that none of you will press against another to ask Him to show Himself. And "*lā tuḍārrūna*" means that none of you will oppose another. It is said: *ḍārrahu muḍārrah* and *ḍirāran*, meaning he opposed him.

His saying, "And the Book will be placed": he said regarding Ibn 'Abbas: it means the Preserved Tablet. Qatadah said: it means the Book and the scrolls in which the deeds of the children of Adam are recorded, so one will take his record in his right hand and another in his left.

"And the prophets will be brought": that is, they will be brought, and He will ask them what their peoples answered them.

"And the witnesses": those who bore witness over the nations from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as the Almighty said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. It is also said that the intended witnesses are those who were martyred in the way of God, who will testify on the Day of Resurrection for those who defended the religion of God. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn Zayd said: they are the guardian angels who bear witness over people concerning their deeds. God the Exalted said: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. The driver drives it to the reckoning, and the witness bears witness against it, and this is the angel assigned to the human being, as will be explained in [Qaf, verse 21 of the said surah].

"And it will be judged between them with truth": that is, with truthfulness and justice.

"And they will not be wronged": Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: their good deeds will not be diminished, nor will their evil deeds be increased.

"And every soul will be paid in full for what it did," whether good or evil.

"And He is most knowing of what they do": in this world. And He, Mighty and Majestic, has no need of a book or of a witness; yet the books are made to testify, as a means of establishing the proof.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 39, verse 71–72:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾. This is an explanation of the full repayment of every soul for its deeds: the disbeliever is driven to the Fire, and the believer is driven to Paradise. Az-zumar (the groups) is the plural of zumrah, like zulmah and ghurfah. Al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "zumaran" means groups scattered, one following another. A poet said:

And you see the people going to his dwelling,
and groups following one another in succession.

Another said:

Until they were ... and group after group.

It was also said: they are driven and urged on with a sound like the sound of the mizmar (a reed pipe). ﴿Until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened﴾: this is the answer to idhā (when), and its gates are seven. This has already been discussed in Surah al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 30 onward, of this edition.]]. ﴿And its keepers will say to them﴾: its singular is khazin, like sadanah and sadin. ﴿They will say to them, as a rebuke and reproach:﴾ ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾, meaning the scriptures sent down to the prophets, ﴿and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾, meaning frightening you of it. ﴿They will say: "Yes."﴾, meaning, indeed they came to us. This is their acknowledgment that the proof was established against them. ﴿But the word of punishment has been fulfilled against the disbelievers﴾, and this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind all together"﴾ [As-Sajdah: 13]. ﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein eternally."﴾, meaning it will be said to them: enter Hell. The discussion of its gates has already passed. Wahb said: the Zabaniyah (angels of punishment) will meet them with maqami' of fire, and they will push them with their maqami', and in a single push a person falls into the Fire in a number equal to Rabi'ah and Mudar. ﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾: its explanation has already been given [[See vol. 10, p. 100 of this edition.]].

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 39, verses 73–75:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who feared their Lord will be driven to the Garden in groups﴾. He means: from among the martyrs, the ascetics, the scholars, the reciters and others, those who feared Allah the Exalted and acted in obedience to Him. Concerning both groups He used the same wording, "driven" (wa-siq). The driving of the people of the Fire is their being expelled toward it in disgrace and humiliation, as is done with captives and those who rebel against the ruler when they are driven to prison or to execution. The driving of the people of the Gardens is the driving of their mounts toward the abode of honour and good pleasure, because they are not taken except as riders, as is done with those among the envoys to some kings who are honoured and esteemed. How far apart are the two drivings!

﴿Until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾. It was said: the wāw here is the wāw of conjunction (ʿatf), coordinating with a previous clause, and the response (jawab) is omitted. Al-Mubarrad said: meaning, they were made happy, and its gates were opened. Omitting the response is eloquent in the speech of the Arabs. He recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. "Tamūtu jamī'uhu" means that a sick person's soul does not leave all at once, but dies gradually, piece by piece, and this is the meaning of "tusāqitu anfusā".]]:

"Had it been a soul that dies all at once...
But it is a soul that falls away, soul by soul."

Here the response of "law" is omitted, and the implied meaning is "it would have been easier." Al-Zajjaj said: "Until, when they reach it" means they entered it, and this is close to the first view. It was also said: the wāw is superfluous. The Kufans said this, but it is an error according to the Basrans. It has been said that the presence of the wāw is evidence that the gates were opened for them before they arrived, because of their honour with Allah the Exalted, and the sense is: until, when they reach it while its gates are already open, as evidenced by His words: ﴿Gardens of Eden, their gates opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]. The wāw is omitted in the account of the people of the Fire, because they were made to stand over the Fire, and its gates were opened after their standing, as a humiliation and a terrifying of them. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Nahhas related its meaning before him. Al-Nahhas said: As for the wisdom in affirming the wāw in the second and omitting it from the first, some scholars have spoken on it with a statement that I know no one has preceded him in, namely that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic said about the people of the Fire: "Until, when they reach it and its gates are opened," this indicates that it was closed; and when He said about the people of the Garden: "Until, when they reach it and its gates are opened," this indicates that it was open before they came to it. And Allah knows best. It was also said that this is the wāw of the eight (wāw al-thamāniyah). This is a custom of the Quraysh, that they count from one, saying: five, six, seven and eight; and when they reach seven they say "and eight." This was said by Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He subjected them to it for seven nights and eight days﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. And He said: ﴿The penitent, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], then He said of the eighth: ﴿those who enjoin right and forbid wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112]. And He said: ﴿They will say, "They were seven, and their eighth was their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. And He said: ﴿Thayyibat and abkar﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5]. The discussion of this has already been given in full in "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 271, first or second edition.]] and also in "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 10, p. 382 onward, first or second edition.]].

I say: Those who hold that the gates of Paradise are eight have used this verse as evidence, and they cited the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you performs ablution and completes (or perfects) the ablution [[Yublighu al-wuḍūʾ: he makes the ablution reach its places. Al-wuḍūʾ is with an open wāw. Yusbigh al-wuḍūʾ: he completes it in the prescribed manner; al-wuḍūʾ is with a dammed wāw. (Margin of Muslim.)]], then says, 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger,' but the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he enters by whichever he wishes." Muslim and others related it. al-Tirmidhi also related this hadith of ʿUmar, and in it he said: "Eight gates of Paradise are opened for him on the Day of Resurrection," with an addition, which indicates that the gates of Paradise are more than eight. We have mentioned this in the book al-Tadhkirah, and their number reaches thirteen gates. We also mentioned there the greatness and vastness of its gates, according to what has been transmitted in the hadith on this matter, so whoever wishes may consult it there.

﴿Its keepers will say to them﴾. It was said: the wāw is redundant, and the sense is "until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, its keepers will say to them: ﴿Peace be upon you; you have been good﴾". That is, in the world. Mujahid said: by obedience to Allah. It was also said: by righteous deeds. Al-Naqqash related it, and the meaning is one. Muqatil said: When they cross the bridge of Hell, they will be detained at a bridge between Paradise and the Fire, and retribution will be exacted from some of them against others for wrongs that were between them in the world. When they have been purified and made pure, Ridwan and his companions will say to them: "Peace be upon you," in the sense of a greeting, "You have been good, so enter it, abiding therein." I say: al-Bukhari related this hadith of the bridge in his Jami' from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believers will be delivered from the Fire, and they will be detained on a bridge between Paradise and the Fire, and retribution will be exacted from some of them against others for the wrongs that were between them in the world. When they have been purified and cleansed, permission will be given them to enter Paradise. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, one of them will know his dwelling in Paradise better than he knew his dwelling in the world."

Al-Naqqash related: On the gate of Paradise there is a tree from whose trunk two springs gush forth. The believers drink from one of them, and their insides are purified; this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord gave them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. Then they wash themselves in the other, and their skins become fragrant. At that moment its keepers say to them: "Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it, abiding therein." The meaning of this is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And they will say: "All praise is for Allah, who has made true His promise to us"﴾, that is, when they enter Paradise they will say this. ﴿And has caused us to inherit the land﴾, that is, the land of Paradise. It was said: they inherited the land which would have been the portion of the people of the Fire had they been believers. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah, Abu Salih, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and most of the exegetes. It was also said: it is the land of the world, with a reversal of order. ﴿How excellent is the reward of the workers﴾. It was said: this is from their own words, meaning: how excellent is this reward! It was also said: it is from the words of Allah the Exalted, meaning: how excellent is the reward of the doers of good, this which I have given them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you will see the angels﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿surrounding﴾, that is, encircling, ﴿the Throne on every side﴾ on that Day, ﴿glorifying their Lord with praise﴾, delighting in that, not worshipping through it; that is, they pray around the Throne in gratitude to their Lord. The word "ḥāffīn" is derived from the "ḥanāfāt" of a thing, its sides. Al-Akhfash said: its singular is ḥāff. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular, since the term applies to them only when they are gathered. The preposition "min" entered upon "ḥawl" because it is a adverbial noun of place (ẓarf), and the verb reaches an adverbial noun of place both with a preposition and without one. Al-Akhfash said: "min" is superfluous, meaning "surrounding the Throne". It is like your saying: "No one came to me," where "min" is for emphasis. Al-Tha'labi said: The Arabs sometimes introduce the particle bāʾ with tasbīḥ and sometimes omit it, so they say: "sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi rabbika" and "sabbiḥ ḥamda Allāh." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], and He said: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74].

﴿And it will be judged between them with truth﴾, between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. It was also said: it will be judged between the prophets who are brought together with the martyrs, and between their nations, with truth and justice. ﴿And it will be said: "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾, that is, the believers will say: "All praise is for Allah for what He has rewarded us with of His blessings and His kindness, and for giving us victory over those who wronged us." Qatadah said concerning this verse: Allah began the first creation with praise of Himself, saying: ﴿And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said, "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾. So it is incumbent to follow Him, beginning every matter with His praise and concluding it with His praise. It was also said: the words "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds" are the words of the angels, and according to this view their praise of Allah the Exalted is for His justice and His judgment. It is related from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the last verse of Surah "al-Zumar" on the pulpit, and the pulpit moved twice.

The tafsir of Surah "al-Zumar" is complete.
